about: THE SPINE of Kapman's written content (Design/content/BRIEF.md), written 4 Oct 2026: the one shared world that the seven region writers, the sea-and-crew writer and the ages writer build on, so that their stories meet. threads: fourteen long stories that cross regions and years, each resting on real history a merchant would feel, with hooks saying what to place where. cast: the recurring people, real and invented. tone, calendar, gods_and_faith: what every writer keeps to. Every dated fact and every historical person has a source; (?) marks what could not be verified; LATER marks a source written long after the thing it tells. Only the spine's writer edits this file and the shared tables (encounters/npc_roles_793.json, encounters/names_placeholder.json). Like all the game's words, a draft for the user to overwrite. Design/content/spine.md says the same in prose.
how_to_use: A story in a places file takes a thread id from here in its 'thread' field. Place what the thread's hook for your port asks for, in your own words, and add stories of your own freely; a hook is a floor, not a ceiling.

A person of the cast is named by id (cast.gervold) in any 'ties' or 'links'. If a cast person's 'home' is one of your ports, write them into that port's people under the id in 'place_id' with the same facts, and tie that row to the cast id with the tie 'kin' and the note 'the same person', so the game has one person and the checker finds both ids.

Never give another invented person the name of anyone in the cast, and never give an invented person a historical person's name and role. Names for your own people: two attested parts of their people, as encounters/names_placeholder.json shows; people ids and roles are those of encounters/npc_roles_793.json.

Threads share flags. A card sets one with the effect 'flag <name>' and any card anywhere reads it as flag.<name> in its 'when' or a 'check'; that is how a card in one region answers a card in another. Use the flags listed under each thread only for the step they name. Flags of your own take your file's name as a prefix. A chain (Design/content/CHAINS.md) keeps its own step flags, ch_<id>_<n>; where a chain's step is also a thread's step, set the thread's flag as well, so that cards outside the chain can answer it.

Gate everything by year. A thread's 'years' are when it is live; a hook's 'when' narrows it. The game starts on 21 June 793: anything earlier is told as news or memory. A card that belongs to one port says so with port.id (Design/content/BRIEF_2.md), and may also be reached from that port's places file (a site's 'do' or a story's beat).

People say days by feasts and moons (calendar), distances by days' sail, odds by a word (sure, likely, doubtful). Prices are in pennies (d) and agree with goods_793.json and Design/economy_and_trade.md.

Texts the chest already holds and a card may give (give_text): alcuin_793, chronicle_793, saxon_vow, aelfric_merchant, irish_viking_terror, dicuil, ohthere, wulfstan, adam, maldon_991, the Hávamál stanzas (havamal_001 ...), Beowulf by fitt (beowulf_01 ... beowulf_43), seafarer, wanderer, deor. Riddles and their sets are riddles_793.json; the thread riddle_road says how they hang together.
The user set the game's music aside for now (4 Oct 2026): write no card, site, reward or unlock that needs music to be heard. A singer is a person who knows the old stories and tells them.
If you need a role, a deed, a variable, a verb or a flag for a thread step that is not here, list it under 'needs' in your report. Do not add it yourself.

threads.title: The black stones and the cloaks
threads.summary: About 789 King Charles asked for a daughter of Offa of Mercia for his son, Offa asked for a daughter of Charles for his own, and Charles in his anger shut his shores to English merchants; the English shut theirs. For some years a Frisian with English cloth, or a Mercian after Frankish wine, trades at the word of a toll man, while Abbot Gervold, who takes the king's tolls at Quentovic and is Offa's friend, carries messages between the two courts. In 796 Charles writes to Offa as a brother about pilgrims, tolls, black stones and the length of cloaks, and in July of that year Offa dies.
threads.truth: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 12 (written 823-867; ed. Loewenfeld 1886 pp. 46-47): Gervold, abbot of Saint-Wandrille from 787, was 'for many years procurator over the kingdom's trade, collecting tributes and tolls in divers ports and cities, chiefly at Quentawich' (our rendering); he was Offa's friend, Offa's letters to him still lay at the abbey, and he went to Offa many times as the king's envoy, the last time over the marriage. The younger Charles asked for Offa's daughter; Offa would not agree unless Bertha, Charles's daughter, were given to his son; the king, 'somewhat moved', ordered that no one from Britain and the English people should touch the shore of Gaul to trade. The Gesta says Gervold's plea stopped the order; Alcuin, writing to Colcu in 790, says the quarrel has gone so far that 'on both sides sailing is forbidden to merchants' and that he may be sent to make peace (Jaffé, Bibliotheca VI no. 14; MGH Epistolae IV no. 7). So the game has the ban real but leaky from 789 to 796. Charlemagne to Offa, 796 (MGH Epistolae IV no. 100; Haddan and Stubbs III p. 496; in part in William of Malmesbury, tr. Giles 1847): pilgrims go free, traders hiding among them 'pay the customary tolls in proper places', the merchants of each realm have the other king's protection; Offa has asked for black stones of a certain length and Charles asks in turn that the cloaks be as long as they used to be; he sends Offa 'a belt, an Hungarian sword, and two silk cloaks' (Giles; the sword is Avar loot). The black stones are usually read as lava quernstones from Mayen (?), by others as dark stone for building or fonts (?). Offa died on 29 July 796 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle). Gervold also roofed his abbey's churches with lead (Gesta c. 12): English lead is the likely source (?).

flags.means: the merchant has been told of the ban by someone who enforces it

flags.name: bs_letter
flags.means: he carries a sealed letter between Gervold's clerk and the wic-reeve of Lundenwic; cleared when delivered

hooks.what: Gervold's toll house. His clerk wants a quiet ship to take a letter to the wic-reeve at Lundenwic while the ban stands (sets bs_letter). An English ship lies under arrest, her wool rotting. After 796 the toll man opens pilgrims' bundles looking for cloaks. Gervold wants English lead for his church roofs.
Saint-Wandrille downstream is Gervold's own house: Offa's letters lie in its chest, and a monk there will say what the quarrel was really about (a marriage).

The wic-reeve Wighelm turns Frankish hulls away, or lets a Frisian land for a gift and a story (sets bs_ban_heard). Cloak-makers ask why the Franks want them longer. Someone wants black stones: quernstones of a set size, a good price for the first cargo after the peace.
Pilgrims waiting for a ship to Quentovic, one of them a trader with a bundle (npc_text_encounters.md sample 8). Also at Sarre and Fordwic.
How far the ban reached is not recorded (?): the game lets the West Saxon wic stay half open, the way round for anyone with nerve. Cast.thiadbod runs English cloth through here.

Skippers argue whether the king's order binds Frisians. Quernstones finished here for the English trade pile up unsold and cheap; English cloth is dear. News of the 796 letter comes with the first ship of that summer (sets bs_peace).
Mayen quern roughouts come down the Rhine. A stone dealer wants to know what length the English king asked for, and will pay for the answer.
Alcuin was here in 790-793 and wrote of the quarrel; the minster's people know his letters. Whether Northumbrian ships were barred too is unknown (?).
A hail in the Channel: an English ship sailing light, turned back from the Canche; or a Frankish king's boat asking whose cloth that is.

The letter's rule outlives both kings: true pilgrims free, traders pay. In 808 the exiled King Eardwulf of Northumbria crosses to the emperor at Noviomagus. In 1027 Cnut wins the same things again at Rome: lower tolls and safe passage for his merchants and pilgrims.
Offa's far shore. Lead from the hills behind comes down to the Dee: the abbot who keeps the Frankish tolls wants lead for his church roofs, and while the ports are shut it cannot lawfully go to him.
In 794 Offa has the East Angles' king beheaded and takes the kingdom: the bishop's town is under a new lord, and his ban on Frankish ships reaches this coast too (?).

threads.title: What was carried off from the holy island
threads.summary: On 8 June 793 heathen men fell on Saint Cuthbert's church at Lindisfarne, killed some of the brethren, took what was precious and carried others off in their ships, youths among them. All that summer the news runs down every coast as fast as a ship and no faster, and what was taken goes north to be sold: a book cover is worth more to its monks than to any Northman, and a boy can be ransomed if someone finds him. Alcuin writes that he will speak to King Charles for the boys; no one wrote down whether any came home.
threads.truth: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 793 (texts_793.json chronicle_793, Giles 1847): 'the harrowing inroads of heathen men made lamentable havoc in the church of God in Holy-island, by rapine and slaughter'. The Chronicle's 'sixth day before the ides of January' is taken as a slip for June, 8 June, the day in the Annals of Lindisfarne. Alcuin's letters of 793: to King Æthelred (MGH Epistolae IV no. 16; texts_793.json alcuin_793) and to Bishop Higbald and the brethren (no. 20), where he says that when King Charles comes home he will go to him and do what he can about the youths led away captive by the heathen. Symeon of Durham (12th century, LATER): some brethren killed, some carried off in fetters, some drowned. Next year heathen men plundered the monastery at Donemuthe, usually taken as Jarrow (?): their leader was killed, a storm broke their ships, and those who swam ashore were killed at the river mouth (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 794). Where the raiders of 793 came from is not recorded (?): the three ships at Portland about 789 were of Hordaland (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 787), and church metalwork of the British Isles, shrine and book mounts cut up as brooches, lies in 9th-century graves of western and central Norway (a whole house-shaped shrine in a woman's grave at Melhus). Buying a book back is attested later: Ealdorman Ælfred and his wife Werburg bought the Canterbury gospels back from the heathen army with pure gold and gave them to Christ Church (the book's own inscription, later 9th century). Captive Christians were found at Birka in 829 (Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 11). Higbald died on 25 May 803. The Lindisfarne Gospels and Cuthbert's body were not taken; the community stayed until 875.

flags.name: lf_trail_north
flags.means: he has learned in a northern port who bought them

flags.name: lf_boy_found

hooks.what: Higbald counting what is gone: the names of the boys, the silver from the shrine, the cover of a gospel book. He will pay ransom in wax, wine or what silver is left, and has a letter for Alcuin (sets lf_knows_boys). The riddle leaves of the 'exeter_storm' set come from this scriptorium.

The king's men saw the sails from the rock and did not come. A thegn is angry or ashamed; King Æthelred is blamed in his own hall (Alcuin's letter blames the court's sins) and is murdered in April 796.

From 794: the wreck of the raiders on the bar, a dead leader, things washed up (a rune-cut stick, a foreign knife). The house where the crew's Beornwine was schooled; a brother there knows the boys' families.
Alcuin's letter to the king read aloud; the minster collecting for ransom; the priest with the letter that reaches Dorestad at the game's start.

The news is thirteen days old on the first day. A priest has a letter from York and wants a book carried to Traiectum. Later a Frisian back from Ripa offers a single psalter leaf, bought for a string of beads.
At Alcuin's hospice of Saint-Josse cast.sigewine waits with Alcuin's answer and a small bag of the king's alms for ransom (?), looking for a ship that goes north.

Cast.thorleif's hall. A woman wears a brooch that was a book mount. Two English boys herd swine; one was sold on. He will sell for silver by weight or a sword, never for prayers (sets lf_trail_north, lf_boy_found).
At the summer market church things are sold as curios: a little house-shaped box, a cup, a strip of gilt. A dealer bought three English boys here in the autumn of 793 (sets lf_trail_north).
Cast.asulf, the dealer in captives, remembers every lot: the English boys went east with a Svea, because Christians cannot be sold south to the Franks. Also at Ripa.

A Svea trader (cast.holmfast or his heir) keeps an Englishman who can tally and read marks. In 829 Anskar finds Christian captives here who are glad of a priest (Rimbert c. 11): one of them may be the last boy of Lindisfarne, a man of nearly fifty.
Beornwine's younger brother Tidwine was an oblate on the island. Finding him is Beornwine's want: he asks for the northern run every spring and counts his share toward the ransom.
A hail from a ship out of the north with church plate under her boards; a boat of monks adrift; the same square sail seen again off the Tyne in 794.
Iona's turn (795, 802, 806); in 875 Cuthbert's people leave the island with his body; a ransomed book given to a church raises standing (riddles_793.json rw_book_gospels).
Hild's house on the cliff watches the sea after 793 and wonders whether to move its books and its saints' bones inland. From 799 a sea chest comes ashore with a leaf of riddles in it.

threads.title: Godfred's market
threads.summary: In 804 Godfred, king of the Danes, comes to Sliesthorp with his fleet and all the horsemen of his kingdom and will not meet the emperor. In 808 he falls on the Obodrites, destroys their trading place at Reric, puts its merchants aboard his ships and sets them down at Sliesthorp, and orders a wall from sea to sea with one gate in it. In 810 two hundred of his ships take a hundred pounds of silver from the Frisians, and before the emperor's army can reach him one of his own men kills him.
threads.truth: Annales regni Francorum 804, 808, 809, 810, 811 (chronicle_793.json). 804: Godfred came with his fleet and all the horsemen of his kingdom to Sliesthorp on the border of his realm and Saxony, promised to meet the emperor and did not. 808: he took Obodrite strongholds and made two thirds of that people pay him tribute, losing his nephew Reginold; he destroyed the emporium on the shore which the Danes called Reric and which by its tolls was of great profit to his kingdom, carried the merchants off with him and sailed to the harbour called Sliesthorp; he had the border of his kingdom toward Saxony closed with a rampart along the north bank of the Eider from the eastern bay to the western sea, with a single gate for wagons and horsemen. 809: talks at Badenfliot came to nothing, Godfred having first sent word by merchants; Thrasco, prince of the Obodrites, was murdered at Reric by Godfred's men (some reckon it 810). 810: a fleet of 200 ships from Nordmannia landed in Frisia, ravaged all the islands off the coast, beat the Frisians in three fights and took 100 pounds of silver as tribute; the emperor marched to the Aller and Weser, and his elephant Abul Abbas, the caliph's gift, died suddenly at Lippeham on the Rhine; Godfred was killed by one of his own following. 811: peace sworn on the Eider by twelve nobles of each people. 812: Hemming dead; Sigfred and Anulo fight for the kingdom and 10,940 men are said to fall. 813: the Danish kings are away making Vestfold submit. Einhard, Vita Karoli c. 14: Godfred counted Frisia and Saxony as his own provinces and boasted he would come to Aachen. The digs agree: the trading place at Gross Stromkendorf on the Wismar bay ends about 810 and Hedeby's harbour begins to grow (?).

flags.name: gf_reric_friend
flags.means: the merchant did a service for cast.dragomir at Reric before 808, or carried word to his kin after

flags.name: gf_paid_share
flags.means: he paid his share of the Frisians' hundred pounds in 810; the Danish fleet lets him be that season

flags.name: gf_warned

hooks.what: The Wends' market under Thrasco, with Danes and Saxons trading in it and a toll that goes to Godfred. Cast.dragomir has a booth: do him a service before 808 (sets gf_reric_friend). In the summer of 808 it burns and its merchants are taken; in 809 Thrasco is killed in what is left. After that the port is gone.

804: the king's fleet and horsemen lie here, and fodder, ale and bread are dear. From 808: the merchants of Reric set down on the shore with what they could carry, Dragomir among them, asking for word of kin; the wall being dug and timbered across the neck; one gate, and the king's man at it.
The king's men gather ships. In 810 a Frisian hull at Ripa is asked whose side she is on: the envoy's card (npc_text_encounters.md sample 9).

The two hundred ships are on the islands. Each terp is told its share of the hundred pounds; cattle are driven inland; three fights are lost. Also at Doccinga, Wijnaldum and Medemelacha (sets gf_paid_share; reads gf_warned).
The count calls out men and boats for the emperor's host in 810; the price of everything an army eats goes up. Then the news that Godfred is dead by his own man's hand, and in 811 the peace.
An easter egg: the army crosses the Rhine at Lippeham, a day downstream, and the emperor's elephant dies there.
The emperor comes to see the ships he ordered built against the Northmen; shipwrights, timber and pitch are wanted.
The king's hall when he is not with the fleet. After 810 Hemming keeps it for two winters; in 812 the hall is half empty of men.
The Danish kings Harald and Reginfrid come with an army to make Vestfold's chiefs submit.
The fleet seen from the masthead off the Frisian islands: run, pay or parley.
Ravn knows men in that fleet and says less than he means. Aldger's kin are on the islands.
Sliesthorp is the gate between the two seas for 250 years: its own coin about 825, a church about 850, burned in 1050, sacked by the Wends in 1066.

threads.title: The end of the Saxon war
threads.summary: The Saxons, baptised by force since 785, rise again in 792 and 793 while the king is busy with the Avars, and the East Frisians rise with them and burn their churches. Year after year the king comes back with fire, takes hostages by the hundred and gives them to bishops and counts far from home; in 804 he empties the land beyond the Elbe of men, women and children and gives it to the Obodrites. A merchant meets this war as grain and horses bought up for the host, as hostages on the Rhine road, and as men who slip north to the Danes.
threads.truth: Annales regni Francorum and Annales Laureshamenses 792-804 (chronicle_793.json). 793: Count Theoderic's force is destroyed in Rustringen on the lower Weser. 794: two armies; the Saxons submit on the Sintfeld and give hostages. 795: the king lays waste the land to the Elbe at Bardowick and takes more hostages than ever before (the Lorsch annals say every third man (?)). 797: the Capitulare Saxonicum softens the first Saxon capitulary (Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae, about 782-785), which had set death for refusing baptism, for eating meat in Lent and for burning the dead, and had forbidden general assemblies. 798: the Saxons beyond the Elbe kill the king's envoys; Thrasco's Obodrites beat them on the Sventana field; 1,600 hostages are taken. 799: Saxons deported with wives and children, their land shared among the king's men. 804: all the Saxons beyond the Elbe and in Wihmodia are moved into Francia with wives and children and the districts beyond the Elbe are given to the Obodrites (Annales regni Francorum 804); Einhard counts ten thousand men with their wives and children, settled in many groups through Gaul and Germany (Vita Karoli c. 7). The Old Saxon baptismal vow names what was forsworn (texts_793.json saxon_vow). A list of 37 Saxon hostages, Westphalians, Eastphalians and Angrians, held by named bishops and counts in Alemannia and to be brought to Mainz at mid-Lent, survives from about 805 (Indiculus obsidum Saxonum Moguntiam deducendorum, MGH Capitularia I no. 115) (?). Widukind twice fled to the Danes (777, 782). Liudger is sent as teacher to the western Saxons at Mimigernaford, later Munster (Altfrid I.23). Whether deported Saxons were sold is not recorded (?): the law forbade selling Christians abroad, and men taken in war were sold all the same.

flags.name: sx_brother_trail
flags.means: the crew's Brunger has word of where his hostage brother was sent (set on the Rhine or at Daventre)

flags.name: sx_brother_found
flags.means: the brother is found at Mogontia about 805; Brunger's want is met or lost

flags.name: sx_carried_fugitive
flags.means: the merchant carried a Saxon out of the king's reach; the king's men may learn of it

hooks.what: The border: Lebuin's church, once burned by Saxons; the host's road east. Grain, horses and salt meat are bought up each May for the army. A Saxon woman asks every boat about a son given as hostage (sets sx_brother_trail).
The Hellweg meets the Rhine: hostages and deported families come down it on foot under guard; an officer wants hulls to carry them upriver or across.

The king's crossing place. In 799 and 804 whole villages wait on the bank to be moved into Francia; a priest reads them the vow again. The archbishop is the king's arch-chaplain and his clerks hold the lists.

About 805 the hostages kept in the south are ordered brought here at mid-Lent. Brunger's brother is on the list, a grown man now who speaks the Alemans' tongue and has a master (sets sx_brother_found).

793: the East Frisians have risen with the Saxons under Unno and Eilrat: churches burned, priests driven out, the count's men dead on the Weser. A priest in hiding wants passage west; Bernlef is baptising dying children. In 794 the priests come back.
Saxons who would not be moved live among the Danes. One asks passage north from a Frisian port (sets sx_carried_fugitive): a good deed to a Dane, a crime to a Frank.
Thrasco's men, the king's heathen allies, sell what they took on the Sventana field; in 804 they are given the Saxons' land and need ploughs, seed and iron.
Saxon families set down on abbey land, speaking to nobody, with a priest set over them. A man asks if any ship goes to the Weser. Also on the Seine above, by Parisius.
The count is away with the host most summers and his steward keeps the tally. In 797 the king's ships are hauled by river and over land into Saxony: boats and men are pressed.
Brunger: baptised by the vow, loyal to the boat, hates the king's men. His brother was given as hostage in 785. He will not eat meat in Lent where a priest can see.

In 841 the Saxon freemen and bondmen rise as the Stellinga for the law of their heathen fathers (Nithard IV.2) and are put down. By 880 Saxon dukes are the realm's shield against the Northmen and die doing it.

threads.title: The cross and the old gods
threads.summary: In 793 the mission to the Frisians is two generations old and still thin: east of the Lauwers the churches burn that year, and the priests come back a year later. Liudger, a Frisian taught at Utrecht and York, breaks the shrines of Fosite on the island at the Danes' edge, baptises in the spring that no one dared speak beside, and gives the blind singer Bernlef his sight, who then baptises dying children when no priest dares the road. A generation on, Anskar carries the same work to the Danes at Sliaswic and the Svear at Birka, in merchants' ships and by the leave of kings who can take it back.
threads.truth: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri, book I (written 839-849; ed. Diekamp 1881). Liudger, born about 742 near Utrecht, learned under Gregory at Utrecht and Alcuin at York (I.9-12); rebuilt Lebuin's burned church at Deventer (I.13-15); was sent to destroy the shrines of the Frisians and brought back the treasure found in them, of which the king took two thirds (I.16); taught seven years at Dokkum until Widukind's rising of 784 (I.17-21); went to Rome and Monte Cassino; in 787 was set over five Frisian districts east of the Lauwers, Hugmerchi, Hunusga, Fivilga, Emisga, Federitga, and the island Bant; crossed to Fosetesland (Heligoland) 'on the border of the Frisians and Danes', saw a dark cloud leave the island as he came with the cross, destroyed Fosite's shrines, built a church and baptised in the spring where Willibrord had baptised three and from which no one had dared draw water except in silence (I.22; Alcuin, Vita Willibrordi c. 10); baptised the chief's son Landric, who became a priest and taught the Frisians for many years; about 793 the East Frisians under Unno and Eilrat burned the churches and drove out God's servants, and after a year Liudger returned (I.22). He was then teacher of the western Saxons at Mimigernaford (I.23), founded Werden on the Ruhr about 799, was made bishop on 30 March 805 and died on 26 March 809. At Helewyret (Holwierde) a matron, Meinsuit, brought him Bernlef, blind three years, 'much loved by his neighbours because he was courteous and knew well how to tell the deeds of the men of old and the wars of kings' (our rendering); healed on the road, he named the villages Werfhem and Wyscwyrd as they came to them, was bound to silence while Liudger lived, learned the psalms from him, and in the rising went from house to house baptising dying infants, eighteen of them (I.25-26). Liudger dreamed of the sun fleeing over the sea from the north with black clouds behind it, and told his sister Heriburg that the Northmen would waste the coast, though not in his days (I.27). Willehad, a Northumbrian, preached at Dokkum about 766, was bishop at Bremen from 787 and died at Blexen on 8 November 789. The Lex Frisionum (about 802), Additio sapientum XI: who breaks into a shrine and takes holy things is led to the sea, and on the sand the tide covers his ears are slit, he is gelded and given to the gods whose temple he robbed. Anskar: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii (about 870; Robinson 1921): to the Danes with Harald in 826, passing Dorstadt (c. 7); to Birka in 829 with merchants, robbed by pirates on the way (c. 10); the prefect Herigar baptised and a church on his land (c. 11); Hamburg burned in 845 (c. 16); Herigar, the rain and the hundred pounds (c. 19); Frideburg and Catla (c. 20); a church at Sliaswic about 850, where many had already been baptised at Dorstadt or Hamburg and others 'were willingly signed with the cross' while putting off baptism (c. 24); lots and the thing at Birka (c. 26-27); the church shut by Count Hovi and opened again, with a bell, and a second at Ripa (c. 31-32). Anskar died on 3 February 865.
