flags.name: ms_fosite_seen
flags.means: he has landed on Fosite's island and seen the spring

hooks.what: 793: the rising. A burned church, a priest hiding in a byre who wants passage to Traiectum (sets ms_carried_priest), Bernlef going from house to house with a bowl of water, the wise woman Notburg saying the old gods have come home. 794: Liudger is back, and nobody is punished who comes to be shriven. Bernlef lives at Helewyret across the Ems mouth (sets ms_bernlef_met).
Boniface's church and the place of the killing; his day is kept on the fifth of June. Liudger passes in spring and autumn. The crew's Aldger was baptised here.

The old lords' terp. A mound where a shrine stood until Liudger's men broke it and carried its silver to the bishop and the king; an old man who was there as a boy tells it without anger or forgiveness.

Saint Martin's and the school. The bishop wants wax, wine and oil, and a ship for letters to York. The books Liudger brought home from York are read here. A priest sent to Emuthon in 794 needs a boat.
Lebuin's grave under the church Liudger rebuilt; Saxon converts and Frankish soldiers at the same Mass.
Liudger is buying land up the Ruhr for his own house of monks at Werden and wants books, a bell and glass.

Fosite's island out in the bight, seen in fog and then clear: a landing, a spring, cattle no one may touch, and since about 791 a small church (sets ms_fosite_seen). A boat of priests asking to be put ashore somewhere they are wanted.

826: Anskar's school for boys he has bought free. About 850: the church by the harbour, traders baptised at Dorstadt who can now hear Mass, others who take the sign of the cross and leave baptism for their deathbed. Mid 850s: Count Hovi has it shut; then it opens again and the king allows a bell.
The younger Horik gives a plot for a second church.

829: Herigar the prefect baptised; Christian captives glad of a priest. 845: the priest driven out. Then Herigar alone at the thing, dry in the rain; the hundred pounds paid to the exiled king's Danes; the old widow Frideburg keeping wine three years for her last hour. About 852: the lots cast in the open field and the old man who says Christ has helped men at sea.

Catla of Birka comes with her dead mother's silver for the poor of Dorstadt, is led round the holy places by devout women, buys four pennies' worth of wine when they are weary, and finds her bag full again (Rimbert c. 20).
Ravn keeps the old gods and Aldger and Beornwine keep the fasts: a fast day and a feast aboard one small boat (npc_text_encounters.md sample 22). Brunger says the vow and means half of it.
Harald Bluetooth baptised about 965 after the priest Poppo carries hot iron; bishops at Schleswig, Ribe and Aarhus from 948; Iceland takes the faith by law in 1000 and keeps a few old customs.

About 854 the Svear come against the Cori: at the siege their lots find no god willing to help, until merchants among them say to ask Christ, and the stronghold yields (Rimbert c. 30). Before that: Gotlanders and Svear living among heathen Curonians, each with their own gods.

threads.title: The blood owed at York
threads.summary: Twenty years before the game begins a Frisian merchant killed a Northumbrian nobleman's young son in a brawl at York, and every Frisian in the city took ship for home for fear of the dead man's kin. Liudger, then a student under Alcuin, was sent home with them, carrying a load of books. No source says the Frisians ever went back: in the game the blood-price was never paid, a Dorestad widow's storehouse stands on what one ship brought away, your own steersman was the boy aboard her, and the richest market of the north is shut to Frisians until someone pays.
threads.truth: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.11-12 (written 839-849; ed. Diekamp 1881): Liudger stayed at York three years and six months; 'as the citizens were going out to war against their enemies it happened that in a brawl the son of a certain count of that province was killed by a Frisian merchant, and for that reason the Frisians made haste to leave the land of the English, fearing the anger of the dead youth's kinsmen' (our rendering). Alcuin 'compelled by necessity' sent Liudger away with those merchants and his own deacon Putul with him, fearing that for love of learning he would go to some other city of that land and be caught by the vengeance; Liudger came home with a fair voyage 'having with him a store of books'; Putul went on to Rome and later came to Gaul with Alcuin as a priest. Diekamp dates it about 773. This is the only notice of a Frisian colony at York; nothing says whether it was restored (?). The custom the story rests on: a killing is settled by wergild paid to the kin before witnesses, or by feud; a Northumbrian nobleman's price in the later 'North People's Law' is counted in thousands of thrymsas (10th-11th century, LATER) (?). York's trading quarter by the Foss and Ouse has yielded continental pottery of the 8th and 9th centuries (the Fishergate digs) (?). The widow's husband, the unpaid price and the watch kept on Frisians are the game's.

flags.name: yk_feud_known
flags.means: the merchant has been told the story by Aldger, Thiadburg or a man of York

flags.name: yk_named
flags.means: the kin at York know whose ship he sails and who is in his crew

flags.name: yk_price_set
flags.means: Ecgwulf has named the price before the archbishop's man

flags.name: yk_paid
flags.means: the blood-price is paid before witnesses: Eoforwic opens to the house and to Frisians

hooks.what: The wic by the Foss: a Frisian hull is looked at twice, asked whose she is (sets yk_named), and may trade only through an English host. Ecgwulf, the dead youth's brother, comes down to the strand. The price can be named before the archbishop's man (sets yk_price_set) and paid in silver, in goods he chooses, or by a service to his lord (sets yk_paid). Old men remember the year the Frisians ran.

Thiadburg's storehouse on the dam: she tells it plainly (sets yk_feud_known), will put up part of the price, and wants her son named in the settlement. Her brother Thiadbod would rather the feud stayed open: York shut is York without rivals for the man who trades there under an English name.
Aldger's home terp and his father's grave; his mother still has the ship's boy's wage from that voyage, unspent. Liudger, who was on the same ship, knows what was said aboard.
The books Liudger carried home from York are in the school's chest: an easter egg, with the year he came.
A monk who was a boy at York's school with Liudger remembers the tall Frisian who did not want to leave. Also at Lindisfarena.
An easter egg: Alcuin's old deacon Putul, who sailed home with Liudger and the merchants, is a priest in Gaul now and can be asked.
Aldger will not go ashore at Eoforwic under his own name, and says why only when asked on a quiet night (sets yk_feud_known). If the price is paid he walks the strand the next morning.
A Northumbrian ship hailed off the Humber whose master asks, pleasantly, what port a Frisian is bound for.

On 1 November 866 the great army takes York and the old feud is nobody's business. In 896 there are Frisians in King Alfred's ships, and three are named among his dead: Wulfheard, Æbbe and Æthelhere (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 897).

threads.title: Silver, stamped and weighed
threads.summary: In the game's first winter the king makes his penny heavier and orders that it be taken in every place, town and market: old coin and foreign silver go to the mint, at a loss the moneyer names. North of the Eider no stamp counts: silver is weighed on a folding scale, nicked to test it and cut to make the weight. And from about this time a third silver comes up the rivers of the east to Aldeigjuborg, Gotland and Birka, coins of the caliphs paid for with furs, wax, swords and people, so that a Frisian who learns all three reckonings can carry the east's silver to the Rhine.
threads.truth: The reform: the heavier denier of about 1.7 g and the pound of 240 are dated to 793-794; the synod of Frankfurt, June 794, c. 5 orders that the new deniers with the king's name, if of pure silver and full weight, be accepted everywhere, with a fine for a free man who refuses them (MGH Capitularia I no. 28; chronicle_793.json 794-06-frankfurt-new-denier). Offa's broad heavy penny follows about 792-793 (793-offa-heavy-penny). Thionville, 805: coin to be struck only at the palace (805-12-thionville-coin). Pitres, 864: a new coinage from ten named mints, Quentovic and Rouen among them. In England one coinage under Æthelstan (Grately, about 928) and one design recalled every few years under Edgar (973). In the north: the first coins of Hedeby, about 825, copy Charlemagne's Dorestad pennies (?); Sigtuna strikes from 995 and Dublin from 997, both copying Æthelred's pennies (chronicle_793.json). Weighed silver: folding scales and lead and bronze weights lie in graves and house floors at Birka, Hedeby, Kaupang and on Gotland; the Norse ounce (eyrir) is about 27 g and eight make a mark (?). The dirhams: the oldest hoard at Staraya Ladoga closes with a coin of 786; a hoard at Peterhof on the Gulf of Finland, about 804-805, has graffiti in Arabic, Turkic runes, Greek and Norse runes (805-peterhof-hoard); a dirham weighs about 2.9 g. Ibn Khurradadhbih (about 885): the Rus bring beaver, black fox and swords. In 839 men who called themselves Rhos and proved to be Svear came to Louis the Pious (839-05-18-rhos-envoys). On Gotland the Spillings hoard, 67 kg, was buried after 870. In 965 Ibrahim ibn Yaqub of Tortosa saw dirhams struck at Samarkand in the market at Mainz (965-ibrahim-hedeby). The stream fails in the 1010s and English pennies, the tribute, fill northern hoards instead (1000-silver-fades). An English curiosity: a gold coin in Offa's name copies an Abbasid dinar of the year 157 of the Hijra (773-774), Arabic lettering and all; the mancus of 30 pence is the dinar's weight in gold.

flags.name: sv_first_dirham
flags.means: the merchant has held a dirham and been told what it is

flags.name: sv_scale
flags.means: he owns a folding scale and knows the northern weights and the nick test; northern buyers stop cheating him

flags.name: sv_moneyer_trusts
flags.means: the moneyer at Dorestad takes his word on foreign silver; the loss is less

flags.name: sv_old_coin
flags.means: he was caught passing old deniers after the reform reached the port

hooks.what: The mint in the upper town. From 794 the moneyer Sigimar takes old deniers and sceattas by weight less his cut, and the toll man refuses them (reform.coin; sets sv_old_coin if you try). The first dirham he is shown is a wonder to him (sets sv_first_dirham, sv_moneyer_trusts).

A mint and the archbishop's clerks: new coin for old at the king's rate, and a clerk who reads out the Frankfurt rule to anyone who argues. Also at Mogontia, where in 965 a traveller from Tortosa marvels at Samarkand silver and Indian spices on a stall.
The Channel mint: English pennies go into the pot and come out Frankish. After 864 one of only ten mints left. Also at Rotomagus.

Offa's moneyers, who sign their coin (Eoba, Ibba and others), change deniers at a loss. An easter egg: a moneyer shows a gold piece with marks nobody can read, copied from a coin a pilgrim brought. Also at Fordwic for Canterbury, and at Gipeswic and Eoforwic.

No coin passes by its face: everything on the scale, old sceattas too. A goldsmith sells a folding scale and teaches the nick and the weights (sets sv_scale). Also at Sliesthorp, where from about 825 small coins copied from Dorestad's are struck.

Holmfast counts twice and weighs once more. Here the merchant first sees silver with the Saracens' writing, whole and cut in halves and quarters (sets sv_first_dirham). Also at Helgo before 800 and at Paviken on Gotland, where men put silver under the floor and say nothing.
The head of the road: furs, wax, honey and people go down the rivers, silver comes up. A dealer pays in dirhams and wants swords. A small hoard lies here (riddles_793.json rw_hoard_ladoga).
Dragomir has a cut dirham on a thong as a curiosity and wants to know what the Franks would give for a bag of them. Also at Truso and Grobin, where amber is weighed against silver.

Ravn tests silver with a knife and his teeth and trusts no stamp; Aldger trusts the king's penny and nothing else. The first time the purse holds three kinds of silver they argue about what the boat is worth.
A Svea ship hailed in the Baltic, low in the water with a chest nobody mentions; a Frisian who will change coin over the gunwale at a worse rate than any mint.
About 900-950 the flood of Samanid silver; after 1010 none, and pennies of Æthelred and Cnut by the ten thousand in the north. A house that knows the scale and the stamp lives through each change.

Gotland's shipwrights and smiths: men who sail east each summer and come home with silver they put under the floor and never speak of. A Gute gives you your penny's weight, not its name (sets sv_scale).
A beach market at the river's mouth: bead and comb makers paid in cut silver. The first place a Frisian sees a coin cut in half on purpose.
Amber weighed against silver at the lake market of the Este; Danish craftsmen with scales; wax and honey from inland. Nobody here has seen a king's penny taken at its face.
The old craft island going quiet as Birka grows: bronze-casters, weights, and things from very far away in a chief's keeping.

threads.title: The hungry years
threads.summary: The game opens in a famine: the harvest of 792 failed across the Frankish lands and in Northumbria, men saw false grain standing in the fields that could be touched but not eaten, and the poor are on every road. At Frankfurt in June 794 the king names the most that may be asked for a measure of oats, barley, rye and wheat and for a penny's worth of bread, makes one new measure for the whole realm, and sells his own grain cheaper still. In 805 and 806 hunger comes again, and the law forbids selling food out of the realm or buying a harvest cheap to sell it dear: the grain that would make a merchant rich is the grain he may not carry.
threads.truth: Famine of 792-794: Annales Laureshamenses and Chronicon Moissiacense 793, Annales Mosellani 792 (a year behind), which tell of people eating people; false grain in fields, woods and marshes (chronicle_793.json 793-great-famine, 793-spring-false-grain). Northumbria: 'these tremendous tokens were soon followed by a great famine' (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 793, Giles 1847: texts_793.json chronicle_793), and blood-red rain from the roof of Saint Peter's at York in Lent (793-spring-york-blood-rain). Frankfurt, June 794, c. 4 (MGH Capitularia I no. 28): no one, in plenty or in dearth, to sell a modius of oats above 1 denier, of barley above 2, of rye above 3, of wheat above 4; twelve wheaten loaves of two pounds for a denier, with more loaves of the coarser grains; the king's own grain, when sold, at about half those prices (?); a new public modius for all (794-06-01-frankfurt-prices). The abundant harvest of 794 ended it. Famine of 805-806: Thionville, late 805: in the present hunger each lord is to feed his own people, sell no grain dear, and send no food out of the realm (805-12-thionville-famine); Nijmegen, March 806: higher price caps for the dear year, and the buying of grain or wine at harvest to sell it later at double named as shameful gain; usury is 'where more is asked back than was given' (806-03-nijmegen-prices; MGH Capitularia I no. 46 c. 11-18, our rendering) (?). A capitulary of about 792-793 orders bishops, abbots and counts to fast, have Masses said and feed the starving poor until harvest (MGH Capitularia I no. 21) (?). Famine and sickness again in 823 (823-famine-epidemic). The game's prices: a sack of wheat 6 d, rye 4, oats 2 in a plain year (goods_793.json, from the Frankfurt caps).

flags.name: hy_fed_poor
flags.means: the merchant sold or gave grain at or under the king's price in a famine port; the church there remembers

flags.name: hy_sold_dear
flags.means: he sold grain above the cap and was seen; the count's men may ask about it

flags.name: hy_ran_grain
flags.means: he carried grain out of the realm in a famine year against the law of 805

flags.name: hy_new_measure
flags.means: he has had his measure checked against the new public modius

hooks.what: The first summer: bread is dear, the church doors are crowded with the poor, and grain is the cargo everyone asks for. From the harvest of 794 the count's steward checks every measure against the new modius (sets hy_new_measure) and the king's price is cried on the dam. Thiadbod has grain in store and is waiting; Thiadburg sells hers at the king's price and says so.
The bishop is ordered to feed the starving until harvest and has not the grain: he will pay in prayers, in a charter, or in the church's silver for a cargo sold fairly (sets hy_fed_poor).

The Rhine is the road grain comes down. The king's estates sell his own grain below the cap; a steward wants hulls to move it and pays in grain. A dealer offers more than the cap, quietly, for delivery after dark (sets hy_sold_dear). Also at Mogontia.
Saint-Denis and the other abbeys feed hundreds at their gates. Men tell of the false grain: ears that stood in the field and came to dust in the hand. Also at Rotomagus and Quentovic.

The same year as the dragons in the sky and the blood on the minster roof in Lent: famine, and then the heathen at Lindisfarne. A cargo of Frankish grain is worth a king's thanks, if a Frankish cargo may land (black_stones). Also at Bebbanburg and Gyrwe.

The terp country grows cattle, not corn, and buys its bread every year: in a famine year a terp will pay in cloth, cheese, hides or a daughter's dowry silver. Also at Doccinga, Emuthon and Medemelacha.
The Danes pay well for grain in any year and very well in this one, and the law of 805 says no food leaves the realm (sets hy_ran_grain). Also at Sliesthorp.
Ship's bread is short and dear; the men watch what the merchant does with a hold full of wheat in a hungry port. Brunger has seen an army eat a district bare.
A boat of people who have left a famine village, asking only to be set down where there is bread.

The king's price outlives the famine as law. Later hungers a house should expect: 823, the cattle plague of 810, the great famine in England in 1005, so hard that no man remembered the like (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle).

threads.title: Swords under the ballast
threads.summary: A Frankish blade is the best in the north and worth three times its price at Sliesthorp or Birka, and since 779 the king's law says no mail coat leaves the realm. In 803 no merchant may be given one, in 805 nothing goes east but by the king's border posts and no arms at all, in 811 churches may not let their swords and mail go to strangers, and in 864 the price of arming Northmen is a man's life. The blades go north all the same, by the hundred; and the emperor's own heathen ally, Thrasco of the Obodrites, cannot lawfully be sold the swords he fights the emperor's wars with.
threads.truth: Capitulary of Herstal, March 779, c. 20: byrnies (bruniae) are not to be sold outside the realm (MGH Capitularia I no. 20). Capitulary for the missi, 803: no arm-rings or byrnies to be given to merchants (chronicle_793.json 803-arms-to-merchants-803). Thionville, late 805, c. 7 (MGH Capitularia I no. 44): merchants going to the Slavs and Avars may go only as far as Bardowick, Schezla, Magdeburg, Erfurt, Hallstadt, Forchheim, Premberg, Regensburg and Lorch, each post under a named officer; they are to carry no arms or byrnies for sale, and if found carrying them lose all their goods, half to the palace and half shared between the officer and the finder (805-12-thionville-border-posts). Boulogne, October 811: bishops, abbots and abbesses are not to give or sell byrnies or swords to any outsider, only to their own vassals (811-10-boulogne-capitulary). Pitres, 25 June 864, c. 25: whoever gives a byrnie, arms or a horse to the Northmen, for ransom or for any price, is a traitor to his country and dies (864-06-25-pitres). The finds: about 170 sword blades inlaid +VLFBERH+T, of the 9th to 11th centuries, most of them in Norway, Sweden, the Baltic lands and Rus, and made by their name and metal in the Frankish Rhineland (Wikipedia 'Ulfberht swords'). Ibn Khurradadhbih, about 885: the Rus bring swords to sell. Prices in the game are the Ripuarian law's: a sword with its scabbard 7 solidi, a byrnie 12 (goods_793.json). Thrasco was the Franks' ally from 795 to his murder in 809 (Annales regni Francorum); that he could get no swords by law after 805 follows from the text, and is not said in any source (?).

flags.name: sw_ran_blades
flags.means: the merchant has carried blades or mail past a toll or out of the realm unseen

flags.name: sw_marked
flags.means: the king's men have his name: the next search is surer and harder

flags.name: sw_buyer_known
flags.means: he knows a buyer in the north by name (cast.asulf, cast.thorleif or cast.holmfast)

flags.name: sw_thrasco_armed
flags.means: he sold swords to the emperor's ally at Reric, against the letter of the law of 805

hooks.what: The smiths' street. A blade may be sold to a count's man and to no stranger; a dealer who asks no questions wants silver by weight, not coin. After 811 an abbey's steward has old mail to be rid of and cannot say so. Also at Mogontia and Diusburg, where the king's men watch the road east.

The toll man's search (the card harbour.tollman.frankish: hide the swords under the ballast). Thiadbod sends blades north in wine casks and has never been caught; a toll man who is cheated remembers (sets sw_marked or sw_ran_blades).
The inland water north from Dorestad, out of the count's sight: where a cargo changes boats at night. Also at Emuthon, the last Frankish landing before the Danes.

Thrasco's men fight the emperor's wars with what they can get. From 805 the border posts are the only lawful road and arms are barred on it: he asks a Frisian for twenty blades and offers wax, honey, furs and his friendship (sets sw_thrasco_armed). A crime, and perhaps a service the emperor would thank you for.
The buyers: a Dane pays double in weighed silver; Asulf pays in captives (sets sw_buyer_known). Also at Ripa. After 864 the same sale is death in the west.
Thorleif wants swords more than silver, and gives a walrus tusk or an English boy for one. Also at Skiringssal, where a smith fits northern hilts to Frankish blades.
Swords go on east: Holmfast buys blades without hilts and sells them at Aldeigjuborg for furs and dirhams.
A king's ship off the Frisian coast stops and searches (npc_text_encounters.md sample 18): the ballast, the casks, the bilge.
Ravn knows who buys and says the Franks made the law because they fear the edge. Aldger will not row a cargo that can hang him. Brunger would arm anyone the king calls an enemy.
From 864 the penalty is death, and the blades still reach the north for two hundred years. A blade sold in 800 can come back in 834 in the hand of a man burning Dorestad.

threads.title: The book road
threads.summary: A book is the dearest thing a small boat can carry: the skins of a herd of calves, a year of a scribe's life, and worth more than the boat. They cross the sea in merchants' hulls with the monks who beg passage: Liudger's from York to Utrecht, Alcuin's from York to Tours, Anskar's forty toward Birka, which pirates took. The same books are what the heathen carry off for their covers and what Christians buy back with gold, so a merchant who learns what a book is worth, and to whom, has a trade no rival understands.
threads.truth: Liudger came home from York about 773 'having with him a store of books' (Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.12, our rendering). Alcuin's verses on York list the authors in its library, and from Tours in 796-797 he asks the king to let him send boys to fetch from York 'the flowers of Britain', the books he lacks (MGH Epistolae IV no. 121) (?). Lul of Mainz and others wrote to Wearmouth-Jarrow for Bede's works a generation earlier (Boniface and Lul's letters) (?). The Admonitio generalis of 789, c. 72, orders schools and corrected books, copied by grown men with all care. Abbot Gervold found his monks 'almost all ignorant of letters', set up a school, and gave Saint-Wandrille a Pentateuch, the minor prophets, Augustine on John in two volumes and a book of homilies (Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 12). What a book costs: the great Bible sent from Wearmouth-Jarrow to Rome in 716 has 1,030 leaves, the skins of some five hundred calves; the game prices a book at 360 d and a hundred leaves of parchment at 60 d (goods_793.json). Lindisfarne's scriptorium made the Gospels now in London about 715-720; they were not taken in 793. Church metalwork from books and shrines lies in graves of western Norway (holy_island). Anskar, sailing for Birka in 829 with merchants, lost to pirates the king's gifts and 'nearly forty books' (Rimbert c. 10, Robinson 1921); at Hamburg in 845 the fire took the library and a Bible the emperor had given (c. 16). The Canterbury Golden Gospels were bought back from a heathen army with pure gold by Ealdorman Ælfred and Werburg his wife and given to Christ Church (its inscription, later 9th century). The gospel book begun on Iona about 800 was carried to Kells (?). In 875 Lindisfarne's people left the island with Cuthbert's body and their books.

flags.name: bk_carried
flags.means: the merchant has carried a book or a book chest safely for a church; monks elsewhere have heard

flags.name: bk_knows_worth
flags.means: a scribe has taught him what a book is worth and to whom: he can price one in a heathen market

flags.name: bk_parchment
flags.means: he has a standing order for calfskin, pigments or wax tablets from a scriptorium

flags.name: bk_lost
flags.means: a book in his care was lost, to water or to thieves

hooks.what: The minster library, the richest north of the Alps. About 797 Alcuin's boys come from Tours to copy what he lacks and need a hull home for a chest of books (sets bk_carried). Sigewine haunts the place. A scribe will price any book you describe (sets bk_knows_worth).

Bede's house: the continent still writes for copies of his books, and the scriptorium wants calfskin, pigments and a ship that does not sink. Beornwine's old schoolroom. Also at Lindisfarena, where the Gospels lie on the altar and a cover is missing from another book.
The school reads the books Liudger carried from York. The bishop wants more and pays in standing, wax or a charter (sets bk_parchment).
Liudger's new house at Werden needs a library from nothing: a first cargo of books up the Ruhr. Also at Colonia and Mogontia, whose schools trade copies with England.
Saint-Wandrille's new school and the books Gervold gave it. Up the Seine, Saint-Denis by Parisius buys parchment by the bundle at the October fair.
The way up the Loire to Tours, where Alcuin's scribes turn out whole Bibles in a clear new hand: a monk wants passage upriver with skins, or down with a finished book for a bishop in the north.
Christ Church's scribes (the riddles of Tatwine). In the later 9th century: a gospel book with gold letters, held by a heathen army for ransom, and an ealdorman who will pay in pure gold.

A book in a heathen house: the cover gone for a brooch, the leaves kept because the pictures are fine. What it is worth here and what it is worth at Lindisfarena are different sums (reads bk_knows_worth). Also at Skiringssal and Ripa.
Anskar's school needs psalters. In 829 he sets out for Birka with nearly forty books and comes there on foot with none: someone has them.
The great gospel book in the making, and after 806 the question of carrying it to Ireland in a boat.
Beornwine can read a book aloud at anchor, and wants to. A wet book is a ruined book: where it rides in a seven-metre boat is a real question (sets bk_lost if it goes wrong).
Books bought back from armies; King Alfred's own books sent to every see about 890; the Exeter book of riddles written about 970 (riddle_road).

threads.title: Dorestad falls, and the rivers with it
threads.summary: From 834 a Danish fleet comes up the river to Dorestad year after year: it burns, kills, carries people off and takes tribute, and in 846 the emperor watches from Nijmegen and can do nothing. The answer the kings find is to give a river to a Northman on his oath to keep the others out: Dorestad to Rorik in 850, and sixty years later Rouen and the mouth of the Seine to Rollo. After the last sack in 863 the Rhine itself leaves Dorestad and its merchants go to Tiel, Deventer and Utrecht; Rollo's Rouen becomes the best market on the Channel.
threads.truth: The Rhine: Annales Bertiniani 834, 835, 836, 837 (tribute taken), 847, 850, 863; Annales Fuldenses 836 (Antwerp and Witla burned), 850, 857; Annales Xantenses 834-873 (chronicle_793.json). Louis the Pious's grant of Rustringen to Harald in 826; Lothar's grant of Walcheren to Harald in 841 and of Dorestad to Rorik in 850, after Rorik had taken it, on condition that he handle the king's dues and hold off the pirates; in 857 Rorik takes land between the sea and the Eider; in 863 Dorestad is sacked for the last time and the fleet goes on up the Rhine; in 867 the people the annal calls Cokingi drive Rorik out; he meets Charles the Bald at Nijmegen in 870 and swears to Louis the German in 873; in 882 his lands go to Godfrid, who is killed in 885. On 26 December 838 a storm flood covers almost all Frisia and 2,437 are counted drowned. Horik, king of the Danes, twice sends word that the fleets are not his (Annales Bertiniani 836, 838). The river: through the 9th century the Rhine's main stream shifts to the Lek and the Kromme Rijn silts (Design/economy_and_trade.md 1.6); the port's 'to' is 863 in ports_793.json. Tiel has a toll by 896 (?). The Seine: Rouen sacked and Jumieges burned in May 841; Quentovic sacked in 842; Nantes on Saint John's day 843; Paris on Easter Day 845 and 7,000 pounds paid; the monks of Saint-Wandrille leave with their relics in 858 (?); Paris besieged 885-886; Rollo granted Rouen in 911 (a charter of 918 names 'the Northmen of the Seine, Rollo and his companions'; the story of the treaty is Dudo's, about 1015, LATER). Noirmoutier's monks leave their island for good in 836 (Ermentarius). Catla's alms at Dorstadt (Rimbert c. 20) fall in the 850s, between sacks.

flags.name: df_buried
flags.means: the house's silver is in the ground at Dorestad (npc_text_encounters.md 2.10)

flags.name: df_warned
flags.means: the merchant brought warning of a fleet up the river before it came

flags.name: df_rorik_man
flags.means: he has sworn to Rorik's peace and pays his toll without complaint

flags.name: df_moved
flags.means: the house has left Dorestad for another river town

hooks.what: Each raid year: loot sold cheap, survivors, a widow, silver put in the ground (sets df_buried). 837: tribute. 846: burned in sight of the emperor. From 850 Rorik's man Eystein takes the tenth and the fleets pass by (sets df_rorik_man). The 850s: Catla's alms, churches full again. 863: the last sack; the heirs of Thiadbod and Thiadburg choose where to go (sets df_moved).
The fleet of 834 comes by Utrecht. In 857 the church is wasted and the bishop goes inland for a lifetime; the trading quarter on the Vecht outlives Dorestad.
The last seasons of the Maas-mouth market: in 836 it burns and is not rebuilt. The pilot's family take their marks elsewhere. Antwerp burns the same year.
837: Count Eggihard and the Dane Hemming, Halfdan's son, die defending the island. From 841 Harald's Danes hold it for the emperor: a heathen lord's peace on a Christian shore.
The palace from which Lothar watches Dorestad burn in 846; where Rorik meets King Charles in 870; held and burned by Northmen in 880-881.
Where Dorestad's trade goes: new plots on the IJssel, old Dorestad names on them. Burned in 882.
The winter after the flood of Saint Stephen's day 838: drowned terps, dead cattle, salt in the wells; everything is wanted and there is nothing to pay with. Along the whole Frisian coast.
King Horik says the fleets are not his, and that he has hanged their chiefs; men in the harbour sell Dorestad cloth and Dorestad people.
841: sacked. A lifetime as the raiders' harbour, where loot and captives are sold. From 911 Rollo's hall: one lord, one toll, thieves hanged, and wine going out to England again.
845: the fair's silver goes to buy the fleet off. 885-886: the siege. The October fair shrinks and moves behind walls. Quentovic is sacked at dawn in 842 and never the same.
The monks gone since 836, the salt pans worked by whoever holds the island; Nantes stormed in 843, Bordeaux taken in 848.

The heir's choices: bury or carry, swear to the Dane or not, stay on a dying river or move. One feud and one friend pass down. By 1020 the merchants of Tiel swear and drink together and judge their own cases.
In 836 the Northmen burn the fort and landing on the Scheldt in the same summer as Witla.
Northmen on the Garonne from 844; the city is taken in 848. Wine still wants buyers, and buyers a way out to sea.

threads.title: The price of England
threads.summary: In 865 a great heathen army lands in East Anglia and does not go home: York falls in 866, kings are killed or driven out, and in 876 the army shares out Northumbria and begins to plough, until Alfred beats it in 878 and there are two laws in England, with hostages given before a man may cross to trade. A hundred years on the raids begin again and the English king pays, ten thousand pounds after Maldon in 991 and more each time, until in 1016 the Dane Cnut is king of all of it, pays off his fleet with seventy-two thousand, and keeps one peace on both shores of the North Sea. It breaks at his death, and in the autumn of 1066 three kings fight for England; the house's story ends at Christmas with a Norman crowned at Westminster.
threads.truth: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 865-1066 (Giles 1847; chronicle_793.json). The army: East Anglia 865, York on 1 November 866, King Edmund killed 20 November 869, Mercia's king driven out 874, Northumbria shared out 876; the Danes swear to Alfred 'on the holy ring' at Wareham in 876 (Giles has 'bracelet'), which they would do for no people before; Edington, May 878; the army crosses to Ghent in 879; Alfred holds London from 886. The treaty of Alfred and Guthrum (880s): no man, free or slave, crosses to the other army without leave, but if they need to trade in cattle and goods it is allowed when hostages are given as a pledge of peace. Lindisfarne's people leave their island in 875. Ohthere and Wulfstan tell Alfred of their voyages about 890. York is a Norse kings' town until 954. The tribute: 10,000 pounds after Maldon in 991 (texts_793.json maldon_991), 16,000 in 994, 24,000 in 1002, 36,000 in 1007, 48,000 in 1012, 72,000 and London's 10,500 in 1018; Saint Brice's day, 13 November 1002; Archbishop Ælfheah killed at Greenwich on 19 April 1012. The treaty of 994 with Olaf (II Æthelred) gives peace to merchant ships in English harbours. London's tolls about 1000 (IV Æthelred): a small boat a halfpenny at Billingsgate, a keel fourpence; the men of Rouen with wine and blubber fish; the Emperor's men, who pay at Christmas and Easter in cloth, pepper, gloves and vinegar (1000-london-tolls). More pennies of Æthelred have been found in Scandinavia than in England. Cnut: king from 30 November 1016; his letter from Rome, 1027, on lower tolls and safe roads for his merchants and pilgrims; died 12 November 1035. In 1066: Edward dies 5 January; Stamford Bridge 25 September; Hastings 14 October; William crowned 25 December. Elsewhere the same years: Utrecht's people burn their own trading quarter in 1006-1007 rather than leave it to the Northmen (chronicle_793.json 1006-tiel-burned); Hedeby is burned in 1050 and sacked in 1066.

flags.name: en_hostage_given
flags.means: the merchant has given a hostage or surety and holds leave to trade across the line between the two armies (878-954)

flags.name: en_paid_share
flags.means: he paid toward a town's share of a tribute

flags.name: en_followed_silver
flags.means: he sold to the fleet that was paid the tribute: the best market of the year and a name for it

flags.name: en_cnut_peace
flags.means: he holds the king's writ of protection under Cnut (1018-1035)

hooks.what: 865: the army's winter camp wants horses and gets them. 869: the king killed. A Danish land for two generations, with weighed silver beside the penny. 991: ravaged before Maldon. From 1017 under Earl Thorkell. Also at Dommoc.

1 November 866: taken. From 876 Danes with land, wives and a market: a town where a Frisian, a Dane and an Englishman can all be cheated in each other's tongue. Its kings strike coin; its hall sets riddles (riddles_793.json ymirs_kin, from 905). In September 1066, Fulford and Stamford Bridge within a week.

871-872: the army winters here and takes its price. 886: Alfred's. About 1000: the toll rules at Billingsgate, read out to every keel. 1009-1012: Thorkell's army on the river and the archbishop killed downstream. 1018: London's own 10,500 pounds counted out. Under Cnut: the king's peace, and the shipmen he keeps.
Thanet ravaged in 980; Thorkell's army lands at Sandwich in 1009 and East Kent pays 3,000 pounds. Also at Fordwic and Dofras. Hamwic is sacked in 980 and Olaf's fleet winters there in 994.
875: the bishop and the people of Saint Cuthbert leave with the body, the books and Oswald's head, and wander seven years.
The great army crosses from England and winters here, selling what it took there.
The Norman duke's town shelters English exiles (King Æthelred in 1013) and sells the raiders' loot; its men pay toll in London on wine and blubber fish. In 1066 the ships are built along this coast.
English pennies everywhere, and men home from England with more than they can spend. Burned by Harald Hardrada in 1050; sacked by the Wends in 1066. Also at Ripa, a bishop's seat since 948.

In 1006-1007 the Northmen burn Tiel and Utrecht's people fire their own harbour quarter. By 1020 the merchants of Tiel judge their own cases; in 1018 Count Dirk beats the emperor's army for his toll at Vlaardingen.
A fleet with a tribute aboard, in a good humour; a ship of Englishmen sold at Rouen or Dublin; in 1066 three fleets in one summer, and the question of whose pilot you are.

For the house: trade across a line of hostages; follow the silver or keep clear of it; a Danish king's peace as the best years the North Sea ever had; and where to stand at Christmas 1066, which is the end of the game.
893: a Danish army winters in the waste city. Restored in 907, then a busy mint and the harbour for Dublin's Norse. In 973 King Edgar comes here and six kings pledge to be his allies by land and sea.

threads.title: The riddle road
threads.summary: Ravn, the Northman who sails with you, sets the first riddle at Dorestad and gives the next when it is answered; after that riddles are had from people in ports, each in its own tongue and its own letters. Some are parts of one thing held in three ports; some are chains, where the answer to one is a word in the next; and the hardest sets end at a place where silver lies in the ground. The Latin riddles go the monks' way, from school to school, and the Norse ones from hall to hall, where a guest who cannot answer drinks for it.
threads.truth: The riddles and their answers are real and are in riddles_793.json and texts_793.json: Gestumblindi's riddles from the saga of King Heidrek (written down in the 13th century, older in substance; Vigfusson and Powell 1883); the wisdom contests of the lays of Vafthruthnir and Alvis (Bellows 1923); the Old English riddles of the Exeter Book (the book about 970, the riddles 8th to 10th century; Tupper 1910); the Latin riddles of Aldhelm of Malmesbury (died 709), Symphosius (late Roman), Tatwine, archbishop of Canterbury (died 734), and 'Eusebius', taken to be Hwaetberht, abbot of Wearmouth-Jarrow from 716. Riddling was a schoolroom and a hall game: Alcuin wrote a dialogue of riddles for Charlemagne's son Pippin about 790 (Disputatio Pippini cum Albino). The sets: aegirs_daughters, three sticks at Skiringssal, Birka and Sliesthorp, for a ship; heidreks_board, three parts of one game, for a board of sea-ivory; exeter_storm, three leaves of one quire at Lindisfarena, Gyrwe and Streonaeshalch, for a hidden cove among the Farne islands; salt_to_pepper, a chain from Quentovic or Dorestad by Herio and Mogontia to Colonia, for the pepper right at the fair of Saint-Denis; and three that open in later ages, alvis_till_dawn (from 860), dellings_door (from 871) and ymirs_kin (from 905), with aldhelm_three_houses (from 928), each ending at a real hoard: Hon, Spillings, Cuerdale, the Vale of York. Gestumblindi's last question, what Odin said in Balder's ear, has no answer a man can give (texts_793.json t-gest-36); the reward for it is the Danish king's favour at Hleidr (rw_favour_hleidr).

flags.name: rd_last_question
flags.means: Ravn has told the merchant what he was asked at Hleidr and could not answer

flags.name: rd_setter_known
flags.means: the merchant has learned that the riddles he is given in the north are passed along by Ravn's old hall-fellows

hooks.what: Ravn's first riddle (r-gest-01, ale) and its reward stanza (r-alv-34). A clerk of the king's mint sells the money riddle, whose reward is toll freedom here (riddle_symphosius_91_pecunia, rw_toll_dorestad). A merchant's son schooled at Utrecht has the anchor. The salt riddle that starts salt_to_pepper may be bought here or at Quentovic.
The cathedral schoolmaster's key (riddle_symphosius_04_clavis). At Noviomagus a clerk of the palace has the river and the fish, and may tell of the riddles Alcuin wrote for the king's son.

A monk on his abbey's business with Aldhelm's salt; a cleric waiting to cross with the ship riddle. The chain runs on to Herio's salt pans (the wine cask), Mogontia (the glass cup) and Colonia (pepper), and pays at the fair of Saint-Denis by Parisius.

Three leaves of one quire of English riddles, scattered when the scriptorium was plundered: here, at Gyrwe and at Streonaeshalch (the third comes ashore in a sea chest from 799). Together they give a landing no other ship uses, among the islands off Bebbanburg.
The scribes of Christ Church sell Archbishop Tatwine's own riddles; one frees a ship of toll here. At Lundenwic the king's toll-reeve gives the ice riddle for the same at London.
The king's skald sells the hard ones. This is the hall where Ravn was set the last question (sets rd_last_question if he is aboard and trusted). Answer everything else and the king's favour follows.

A ferryman on the Schlei has one of Aegir's daughters; a Vestfold skipper at Skiringssal and a skald at Birka have her sisters. The men who give them have all sat on a bench with Ravn (sets rd_setter_known).
The Svear king's skald; from 871 the chain of Delling's door begins and ends here, by Paviken, Aldeigjuborg and Ahus, and leads to silver under a floor on Gotland.
The chain of Ymir's kin among the Norse halls of Dublin and York and at Hi, ending at the silver by the Ribble.
A master hailed at sea gives a riddle for news (riddles_793.json acquire 'sea'): Norse, English or Irish by the ship.

Reading with the crew (npc_text_encounters.md sample 23): Ravn reads a rune stick in part, Beornwine a Latin leaf in part, and the merchant finishes it. Ravn never gives an answer, only the next riddle.
The later sets open by year (860, 871, 905, 928). An heir inherits the chest, the solved riddles and whatever Ravn told the house before he died.

threads.title: The count's day
threads.summary: The boat was bought on the count's silver: four hundred and eighty pennies, two pounds, to be paid at Michaelmas. Every generation of the house has such a day: a debt to a count, then to the Dane who holds Dorestad's toll, then to a bishop, a count of the coast, a sworn company of merchants. The house lives as long as it can meet the day, or find someone who will stand surety for it.
threads.truth: The debt is the game's own device: 480 d owed for the ship to a Frankish count, due in 365 days (trade_rules.json start; the user's decisions of 26 Sep and 4 Oct 2026: 480 d by Michaelmas on the easy terms). What it rests on: 240 pennies make a pound from the reform of 793-794; a small sea-going boat at about two pounds is the game's own price (?). Michaelmas, 29 September, is among the feasts the council of Mainz ordered kept in 813 (c. 36), and autumn after harvest is the usual term for dues (?). A count holds the king's court and toll in his district; no count of Dorestad is named for the 790s, so cast.folcbert is invented. Lending at interest was forbidden to everyone by the Admonitio generalis of 789 (c. 5), and the capitulary of Nijmegen, 806, says usury is where more is asked back than was given (MGH Capitularia I no. 46 c. 11) (?): so the count's silver comes back as the sum and a service, a pledge, or a share, never as interest by name. Pledges, sureties and oath-helpers are the ordinary law of every people here. The split tally stick as the record is the game's (attested later; for the 790s (?)). Who holds Dorestad after the counts: Rorik, 850 to about 873, on condition of handling the king's dues (Annales Fuldenses 850); Godfrid, 882-885; then the bishops of Utrecht and the counts of the coast. In 1018 Count Dirk beats the emperor's army to keep his toll at Vlaardingen, and about 1020 the merchants of Tiel 'swear and drink together' and judge their own cases, to the monk Alpert's disgust (chronicle_793.json 1018-07-29-vlaardingen, 1020-tiel-merchants).

flags.name: db_extension
flags.means: the count has given a delay past the day, for a service or a gift; one time only for each creditor

flags.name: db_service
flags.means: the merchant owes the count an errand in place of part of the silver; cleared when done

flags.name: db_surety
flags.means: someone stands surety for the house: the bishop, the widow Thiadburg, or a sworn company

flags.name: db_bought
flags.means: the debt has been bought by another (cast.thiadbod), who now holds the tally

hooks.what: The count's hall and his steward Hartwin with the tally. At Michaelmas the reckoning: paid in the king's new pennies, in goods he will take, or in a service (sets db_service). The widow Thiadburg lends on goods left in her storehouse (sets db_surety); her brother Thiadbod offers to take the debt off the count's hands (sets db_bought). From 850 the day is Rorik's and his man Eystein keeps it.
When the king keeps a feast at the palace the count is there: the one place to ask for a delay to his face, with a gift fit for the company (sets db_extension).
The bishop will stand surety for a house that carries his letters and sells him wax fairly (sets db_surety). After Dorestad is gone the house's reckoning day is here or at Daventre.

An errand for the count: English hounds and a cloak of the old length for his table and his back. Each region may hold ONE such errand for the count of Dorestad, a thing he could really want from there: a falcon and a walrus-hide rope from the north, glass from Colonia, amber for his wife from the Baltic shore, wine from the Seine.
The men's shares against the count's day: a crew paid late at the venture's end, or a count paid late (npc_text_encounters.md sample 20). Brunger would rather the count went unpaid.
A gale in the last week before Michaelmas with the count's silver in the hold as cargo: what goes over the side.

Each heir begins with a day of his own. 834-863: debts in a town that burns. 850: the Dane's toll. After 863: a new town and a new lord. About 1020: a seat among the sworn merchants of Tiel, who answer for each other's debts.

cast.name: Ravn
cast.dates: born about 750; with the house from the first day, 21 June 793
cast.seat: the trader's seat, and the first teacher
cast.trait: Dry and watchful; keeps his word and his own counsel; pious to the old gods without talking of them; sets riddles instead of giving advice.
cast.want: To stand in the hall at Hleidr once more and hear the last question asked, the one he was set there as a young man and could not answer (texts_793.json t-gest-36).
cast.fear: To die among Christians unable to speak, be signed with their cross and put in their ground.
cast.voice: Short sentences with a picture in them; never says where he is from, and turns the question into a riddle.
cast.looks: About forty-five, lean, weathered, fair hair gone grey and tied back, a short beard; a plain dark wool tunic and sea cloak, a knife and a whetstone at his belt, a small leather bag of rune-cut sticks.

ties.note: knows him of old and does not say how
ten years in the same boat; they argue about gods only on fast days
will not sit at a table with a dealer in people; the reason is his own

cast.source: invented; the user's guide and teacher (decision of 26 Sep 2026: a Northman, origin left open, aloof, pious to the old gods, dry); gives the first riddle (riddles_793.json r-gest-01)

cast.name: Aldger
cast.dates: born about 761
cast.trait: Steady, sparing with words, counts tides in his head; baptised as a child at Doccinga and keeps every fast.
cast.want: To see the blood-price paid at Eoforwic, so that he can walk its strand again under his own name: he was the boy on the ship that fled in 773.
cast.fear: The dead youth's kin; and fog on a lee shore.
cast.voice: Dry Frisian: says the worst first and plainly, then what can be done about it.
cast.looks: A little over thirty, broad, short-legged, sandy hair and a cropped beard, eyes narrowed from watching water; a short Frisian cloak, a wooden cross on a thong, the steering oar's callus on his right hand.

ties.note: sailed for her husband Radger as a boy and still does her errands unasked
was on the ship of the man who killed Ecgwulf's brother
Liudger taught at Doccinga for seven years and knows his family

cast.source: invented; the flight of the Frisians from York about 773 is Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.11-12

cast.name: Brunger
cast.dates: born about 765 on the Weser
cast.seat: the mate's seat: he speaks for the oars
cast.trait: Strong, loyal to the boat, slow to speak and slower to forgive; said the baptismal vow because the law is baptism or death.
cast.want: To find his younger brother, given as a hostage when their district submitted in 785 and sent to a lord in the south; the trail ends at Mogontia about 805.
cast.fear: The king's men, and a priest asking what he ate in Lent.
cast.voice: Few words, Saxon ones; a proverb when he is pleased, silence when he is not.
cast.looks: Late twenties, tall and heavy in the shoulder, long fair hair, a moustache and no beard; an undyed tunic, a long knife (a seax) across his belly.

ties.note: the count led the levy that burned his village; the count does not know him
the boy reads; Brunger thinks reading is how his brother will be found

cast.source: invented; the hostages and the vow are chronicle_793.json and texts_793.json saxon_vow

cast.name: Beornwine
cast.dates: born about 775
cast.seat: the lookout's seat, and the reader
cast.trait: Quick, sharp-eyed, bookish and homesick: schooled as an oblate at Gyrwe, he left before his vows and reads Latin slowly but truly.
cast.want: To find his younger brother Tidwine, an oblate of Lindisfarena carried off on 8 June 793, and bring him home.
cast.fear: The heathen men; and that he left the cloister and God has noticed.
cast.voice: Talks too much when afraid; quotes a psalm and then is embarrassed.
cast.looks: Eighteen, thin, dark hair growing out of a cropped head, ink-stained fingers that the oar has since blistered; a monk's cast-off tunic cut short, a wax tablet in his shirt.

ties.note: his younger brother
the bishop knows the family and sends him word
taught him his letters at Gyrwe

cast.source: invented; the youths carried off are Alcuin's letter to Higbald, 793 (MGH Epistolae IV no. 20)

cast.name: Folcbert
cast.dates: born about 748; count over the Dorestad district in the 790s (no count there is named in the sources)
cast.trait: A soldier who holds a court because the king says so: fair by his own lights, bored by merchants, away with the host most summers.
cast.want: His silver back at Michaelmas, or something better than silver: a service, a rare thing for his table, a favour he can show the king.
cast.fear: The king's envoys finding his toll short or his court bought.
cast.voice: Brief and loud, a man used to being obeyed outdoors; calls every Frisian 'shipman'.
cast.looks: Mid forties, thick-set, short brown hair and a long moustache in the Frankish way, a red cloak pinned on the right shoulder over a mail-worn tunic, leg bindings, a sword he never takes off.

ties.note: Hartwin is his steward and keeps his tallies
takes Thiadbod's gifts and thinks well of him
count and bishop share the district and dispute every fine
