cast.name: Hartwin
cast.dates: born about 740
cast.trait: The count's steward: remembers every debt in the district and cuts each on a split tally stick; honest, and proud of being hard to cheat.
cast.want: The tally to close clean on the day; failing that, a pledge he can hold in his hand.
cast.fear: Being blamed for his lord's shortfalls; fire in the hall where the tallies hang.
cast.voice: Counts aloud, in dozens and scores; never raises his voice.
cast.looks: Past fifty, thin, grey, clean-shaven, a plain brown cloak with a bronze pin, a bundle of notched sticks at his belt and a small pair of scales in a box.

ties.note: his lord for twenty years
the steward and the moneyer check each other's weights

cast.source: invented; the split tally is the game's device for the debt (tallies are common later; for the 790s (?))

cast.name: Thiadbod
cast.dates: born about 755; his sons and grandsons keep the house after him
cast.trait: The rival: a bigger ship, a dam head of his own, a gift for every officer; never breaks a law where he can be seen.
cast.want: To be the first Frisian house on the river, and to own the player's debt so as to own the player.
cast.fear: A search of his wine casks on the wrong day; a younger, luckier skipper.
cast.voice: Friendly, generous with news that is a week old, never with news that is fresh.
cast.looks: About forty, well fed, combed fair beard, a long blue cloak of the best Frisian cloth with a silver pin, rings on two fingers, soft boots that have never hauled a boat.

ties.note: his elder sister; she does not trust him with her storehouse
gives the count hawks and wine
blades went north on credit; Asulf is owed captives or silver
the reeve lets his ship land when others are turned away

cast.source: invented: the rival Frisian skipper; the name is Thiad- (as in Thiadgrim, Liudger's father) and -bod (as in Radbod)

cast.name: Thiadburg
cast.dates: born about 750; widowed about 785
cast.trait: Keeps the storehouse on the dam her husband built with what one ship brought away from York; lends on goods, forgets nothing, gives to the church without saying so.
cast.want: The blood-price her husband Radger owed at Eoforwic paid before she dies, so her son can trade there; she will back a skipper who takes it.
cast.fear: That her brother Thiadbod will have the storehouse when she is dead.
cast.voice: Plain, quick, a little amused; asks what a thing weighs before she asks what it cost.
cast.looks: A little over forty, upright, a white linen head-cloth, a dark gown with two round brooches and a string of amber and glass beads, a ring of keys at her belt.

ties.note: her younger brother, and her rival for the dam head
her dead husband killed his brother in a brawl in 773; the wergild was never paid
he was her husband's ship's boy

cast.source: invented: the widow with a storehouse. Her husband is the 'certain Frisian merchant' of Altfrid I.11, whom the source does not name; the name Radger is ours

cast.name: Sigimar
cast.dates: born about 752
cast.trait: The moneyer of the king's mint in the upper town: exact, incurious about people, curious about every coin; the first man on the Rhine to puzzle at a dirham.
cast.want: Old pennies and foreign silver brought to him and not to the scales of a Dane; to know what the strange lettering says.
cast.fear: A light coin with his mint's name on it; the king's law of 794 and the men who enforce it.
cast.voice: Says a weight, then a loss, then nothing; warms only to a coin he has not seen before.
cast.looks: About forty, stooped, burn-scarred forearms, a leather apron, a cap, a touchstone on a cord round his neck; behind him the anvil, the dies and a guard.

ties.note: they check each other's weights
the Svea weighs silver the moneyer says must be struck

cast.source: invented; the mint at Dorestad and the reform of 793/4 are npc_text_encounters.md 1.1 and chronicle_793.json 794-06-frankfurt-new-denier. Frankish coin of this time names the mint, never the moneyer

cast.name: Gerlef
cast.dates: born about 745
cast.trait: The pilot of the Maas mouth: knows where the channel went after each winter's floods, and the Thames to the Strand; tells the truth about water and lies about his age.
cast.want: A son or a pupil to take the marks from him before his eyes go.
cast.fear: Going blind; a new sandbank where his father's channel was.
cast.voice: Talks to the water more than to the merchant: 'she shoals here', 'she runs north of the bank now'.
cast.looks: Nearly fifty and looks older, wiry, white stubble, a salt-stiff hooded cloak, a sounding pole taller than himself and a lead on a line with tallow in its foot.

ties.note: Thiadbod pays him by the year, so others wait
taught Aldger the Thames marks

cast.source: invented: a pilot. The sounding lead and pole are in research_trade_seasons_and_hints.md 4; Witla burns in 836 (Annales Fuldenses)

cast.name: Notburg
cast.dates: born about 730
cast.trait: The wise woman of the Ems mouth: herbs, births, knots against fever, the right words at a spring; baptised twice by order and unmoved both times.
cast.want: The old customs left alone at the edges: the silence at the spring, a feast at the graves in the dark of the year.
cast.fear: Not the priests, who only talk: the count's men, and being forgotten.
cast.voice: Kind, exact, a little mocking; calls Liudger 'the Utrecht boy'.
cast.looks: Past sixty, small, straight-backed, grey plaits under a dark cloth, a pouch of dried herbs, a knotted cord and a small knife at her girdle, a staff of ash.

ties.note: they are of an age and know the same stories
he breaks what she tends, and asks after her health

cast.source: invented; what she does is the list of the Indiculus superstitionum (10 amulets and knots, 11 springs, 12 incantations) and Fosite's silent spring (Altfrid I.22)

cast.name: Sigewine
cast.dates: born about 758
cast.trait: A Northumbrian monk who carries Alcuin's letters and brings back books: a bad sailor, a good walker, incapable of passing a library.
cast.want: A ship that sails when it says it will; a copy of a book York lacks.
cast.fear: The sea; arriving with a letter after the man it is for has died.
cast.voice: Apologises, then asks for exactly what he needs; complains of the cold like a scribe in a margin.
cast.looks: Mid thirties, tall and stooping, tonsured, a patched black cowl, a leather letter case under his arm and a wax-sealed satchel he will not put down.

ties.note: his old master, whose letters he carries
taught the boy his letters at Gyrwe
brings him Alcuin's answers
crosses free at Quentovic by the abbot's word

cast.source: invented: the monk carrying letters. Alcuin's letters went by such men and by Frisian ships (reputation_793.json carried_letters); the deacon Putul who went home with Liudger (Altfrid I.12) is a real one

cast.name: Wighelm
cast.dates: born about 750; wic-reeve under Offa and then Coenwulf
cast.trait: The king's wic-reeve on the Strand: witnesses every sale, enforces the ban on Frankish ships with regret and a private price.
cast.want: The ports open again, and the first good cargo after the peace to pass through his hands.
cast.fear: King Offa, who beheaded a king in 794; after 796, the men who remember whose reeve he was.
cast.voice: Courteous, slow, asks the same question twice to see if the answer changes.
cast.looks: About forty-five, grey-fair, clipped beard, a green cloak with a gilt disc brooch, a short sword, a rod of office, two armed men behind him.

ties.note: they write to each other through the ban
both are Offa's men in the south
takes his gifts

cast.source: invented; the office is the wic-reeve of Lundenwic in the laws of Hlothhere and Eadric c. 16. Offa had King Æthelberht of East Anglia beheaded in 794 (chronicle_793.json)

cast.name: Ecgwulf
cast.dates: born about 755
cast.trait: A Northumbrian thegn whose elder brother, a nobleman's son, was killed by a Frisian merchant in a brawl when Ecgwulf was a youth; patient, correct, and still counting.
cast.want: The blood-price, paid before witnesses, or a Frisian of that house within reach.
cast.fear: Dying with it unpaid, which would shame his sons.
cast.voice: Formal and quiet; names his brother every time he speaks of Frisians.
cast.looks: Late thirties, tall, a scar through one eyebrow, long hair and a full beard, a dark red cloak with a silver ring pin, a pattern-welded sword in a worn scabbard.

ties.note: her husband struck the blow in 773
the boy on the ship is a man now
his lands lie under the archbishop's protection

cast.source: invented; the killing is Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.11: the son of a certain count of that province was killed in a brawl by a Frisian merchant, and the Frisians fled 'fearing the anger of the dead youth's kinsmen' (our rendering)

cast.name: Tidwine
cast.dates: born about 781; carried off from Lindisfarena on 8 June 793
cast.trait: An oblate of twelve who could write a fair hand: sold north, he lives by being useful and forgets his English a word at a time.
cast.want: At first, home. Later, he is not sure: he has a place, a skill and perhaps a wife among the heathen.
cast.fear: Being sold again.
cast.voice: As a boy, whispers; as a man, speaks Norse with an English turn and Latin only in his sleep.
cast.looks: As a boy: small, cropped hair, a torn habit, bare feet, a thrall's collar of rope. As a man of forty: a trader's servant in northern dress who still holds a stick like a pen.

ties.note: his elder brother
taken on Thorleif's ship (?)
bought for his tallying and kept
the bishop's own oblate

cast.source: invented: one of the youths of Lindisfarne whom Alcuin hoped to ransom (letter to Higbald, 793). Christian captives were at Birka in 829 (Rimbert c. 11)

cast.name: Asulf
cast.dates: born about 755
cast.trait: A dealer in captives who thinks himself an honest man: feeds his lots, keeps families together when it costs nothing, remembers every sale.
cast.want: Frankish blades, which buy more captives than silver does; and a quiet trade.
cast.fear: A king who decides the trade is his; sickness in the pen.
cast.voice: Says less than he means; names prices in ounces of silver and never haggles twice.
cast.looks: Around forty, stout, a plaited beard, a good grey cloak with a silver ring pin, an arm ring he cuts pieces from to pay, a switch of hazel in his hand.

ties.note: sells what the king's wars take
is owed for a lot Thiadbod took on credit
buys what Thorleif brings home
Ravn will not sit with him

cast.source: invented: a dealer in captives. Hedeby and Birka were markets for people; Anskar bought Danish and Slav boys (Rimbert c. 15)

cast.name: Thorleif
cast.dates: born about 760
cast.trait: A ship's chief of the west coast who farms in winter and sails in summer; was west over the sea in 793 and came home rich in things he has no use for.
cast.want: Swords and a second ship; a name that outlasts him.
cast.fear: A summer with nothing to show; his own crew's opinion.
cast.voice: Understates everything: a sacked church is 'a good landing'. Laughs before he threatens.
cast.looks: Early thirties, big, wind-burned, red-fair hair and beard, a blue tunic with tablet-woven braid, a silver neck ring, an axe with a long haft; on his wife's breast a brooch that was once a book's mount.

ties.note: sells him the people he takes
they know each other of old
nothing, as he sees it: he took the boy and sold him

cast.source: invented. Who raided Lindisfarne is not recorded (?): western Norway is the usual guess, from the Hordaland ships of 789 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 787) and the church metalwork in graves there

cast.name: Dragomir
cast.dates: born about 760; of Reric until 808, then set down at Sliesthorp
cast.trait: An Obodrite trader in honey, wax, furs and people: careful with oaths, generous at table, never forgets a service or a slight.
cast.want: Before 808: Frankish iron and a friend in the west. After: word of his kin, and a way home that does not pass Godfred's gate.
cast.fear: The Danish king's ships in the bay; after 808, being counted a Dane's man by his own people.
cast.voice: Speaks through an interpreter until he trusts you, then in rough Danish; will not swear lightly, and says why.
cast.looks: About thirty-five, wide-faced, brown hair cut round, a moustache, a long belted tunic and a fur-edged cap, a ring of twisted silver wire at his temple (his wife wears several), a wax tally in his hand.

ties.note: his prince, whose toll he paid
the king who burned his booth and carried him off
they sold in the same market and now in the same harbour

cast.source: invented: one of the merchants Godfred moved from Reric to Sliesthorp in 808 (Annales regni Francorum 808). The name is two Slavic parts, Drago- and -mir (Dragovit of the Wilzi; Slavomir of the Obodrites). Temple rings are found in later Slavic graves (?)

cast.name: Holmfast
cast.dates: born about 758; his son keeps the booth after him
cast.trait: A Svea trader who counts everything twice and weighs it a third time: furs east to west, silver west to east, and no word wasted on either.
cast.want: A steady buyer on the Rhine for furs and wax, and Frankish glass and blades to take east.
cast.fear: Short weight; the ice coming early with his goods on the wrong side of it.
cast.voice: Numbers first. Repeats your offer back to you slowly, then is silent until you raise it.
cast.looks: About thirty-five, spare, pale-eyed, a trimmed beard, a fur-trimmed cap and a belted coat of eastern cut, folding scales in a round bronze case and a bag of lead weights at his belt.

ties.note: the scale against the stamp
bought the boy for his tallying; owes him, by his own reckoning, nothing
they have traded wax for years without a quarrel

cast.source: invented: a Svea trader. Men of Birka had been to Dorstadt (Rimbert c. 27); scales and weights lie in Birka's graves; the name is Holm- and -fast, both common on the rune stones of Uppland

cast.name: Eystein
cast.dates: born about 815; Rorik's man at Dorestad from 850
cast.trait: A Dane taking a Frankish king's toll for a Danish lord: exact, a little ashamed of the work, proud of keeping other pirates off the river.
cast.want: The toll full, so that his lord keeps his grant; a Frisian wife and a house that does not burn.
cast.fear: The next fleet being bigger than his lord's; being left behind when Rorik sails.
cast.voice: Frisian with Danish bones in it; says 'the king's tenth' and means two kings.
cast.looks: Mid thirties, fair, a moustache, a Frankish cloak over a northern tunic, an arm ring beside a toll man's tally stick; he may wear a small cross for the day's business.

ties.note: his lord
Thiadbod's grandsons pay him well

cast.source: invented: the toll man under Rorik. Rorik was taken back into the king's faith on condition that he handle the taxes and the king's dues honestly and hold off the Danish pirates (Annales Fuldenses 850)

cast.name: Gervold
cast.dates: bishop of Evreux from about 785; abbot of Saint-Wandrille from 787 (or 788) until his death in 806 or 807
cast.trait: A king's officer more than a monk: the procurator who takes the tolls of the Channel ports, Offa's friend, by his own monks' account no great scholar and a builder.
cast.want: The two kings at peace so the tolls flow again; English lead for the roofs of his abbey's churches.
cast.fear: The king hearing that the tolls are short, or that his friendship with Offa was worth more to him than his office.
cast.voice: Smooth and exact; names sums and saints in the same breath; never says no at once.
cast.looks: About fifty-five, portly, tonsured, a fine dark cowl with a silver cross, an abbot's staff carried by a boy, a seal on a cord and a clerk with tablets at his elbow.

ties.note: they write to each other while the ports are shut
each is spoken of as the man to make the peace with Offa
lets Alcuin's letter-carrier cross free

cast.source: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 12 (ed. Loewenfeld 1886): procurator 'for many years', taking tolls 'chiefly at Quentawich'; many embassies to Offa, the last over the marriage; roofed Saint Peter's and Saint Michael's with lead and set up a school. Dates: Wikipedia 'Gervold' (bishop 785, abbot 787, died 806 or 807)

cast.name: Alcuin
cast.dates: born about 735 at York; at Charles's court from 782; in Northumbria 790-793; back at court by 793; abbot of Saint Martin's at Tours from 796; died 19 May 804
cast.trait: The best teacher of his age and a tireless writer of letters: homesick for York's books, fond of riddles and pet names, scolds kings and bishops alike.
cast.want: His letters carried and answered; the youths of Lindisfarne ransomed; York's books copied for Tours.
cast.fear: That the sack of Saint Cuthbert's church is a judgement on Northumbria's kings, and the beginning of worse.
cast.voice: Warm, learned, turns every piece of news into a lesson; met mostly as a letter read aloud.
cast.looks: Nearing sixty, slight, tonsured grey, a deacon's plain dark dress, ink on his fingers, a pile of wax tablets and a boy to carry them; never seen without a book.

ties.note: his pupil at York for three years and a half
his pupil, whom he scolds as archbishop
writes to him after the raid
writes to him in his exile
who carries his letters

cast.source: Alcuin's letters (MGH Epistolae IV, ed. Dümmler 1895) nos. 7, 16, 20, 100, 124; Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.10-12; dates from Wikipedia 'Alcuin'. He is at court, not in a port: a merchant meets him on a feast at Noviomagus, or by letter; from 796 he is at Tours, up the Loire from Namnetis. The abbey of Saint-Josse by Quentovic is said to have been given him about 792 as a hospice for English travellers (?)

cast.name: Higbald
cast.dates: bishop of Lindisfarne from 780 or 781 until his death on 25 May 803
cast.trait: The bishop who was there on 8 June 793 and stayed: counts what is gone, writes to Alcuin, keeps the brethren on the island.
cast.want: The youths found and bought back; the shrine made whole; wax and wine for the altar.
cast.fear: A second sail; the brethren asking to leave the island.
cast.voice: Tired and exact; lists what is missing on his fingers.
cast.looks: Past sixty, gaunt, tonsured white, a patched habit and a plain wooden staff since the good one was taken; behind him a church with its doors off.

ties.note: Alcuin's letters of 793 are to him
one of the youths carried off
knows the brothers' family

cast.source: Alcuin to Higbald, 793 (MGH Epistolae IV no. 20); Wikipedia 'Higbald of Lindisfarne' (bishop 780/781, died 25 May 803); chronicle_793.json 803-05-25-higbald

cast.name: Liudger
cast.dates: born about 742 near Utrecht; priest 777; teacher of five East Frisian districts from 787; driven out about 793 and back within a year; founds Werden about 799; bishop at Mimigernaford (Munster) 30 March 805; died 26 March 809
cast.trait: A Frisian nobleman's son taught at Utrecht and York: gentle with people, hard on shrines, always carrying books.
cast.want: Priests, books and a bell for the Frisians and the western Saxons; a house of monks on his own land at Werden.
cast.fear: The Northmen: he dreamed of the sun fleeing over the sea from the north with black cloud behind it, and wept.
cast.voice: Plain Frisian with a little of York's English in it; asks before he tells.
cast.looks: About fifty, tall and spare, tonsured, a travel-stained cloak over a priest's tunic, a book satchel, a small cross of bronze; he rides a horse and leads it through villages.

ties.note: his master at York
gave him back his sight and taught him the psalms
baptised him on Fosite's island and made him a priest
breaks what she tends
Utrecht's bishop is his old school's lord

cast.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri, book I (ed. Diekamp 1881); Wikipedia 'Ludger' for the dates of 805 and 809; chronicle_793.json 809-03-26-liudger

cast.name: Bernlef
cast.dates: of Helewyret (Holwierde) in Fivelgo; blind three years, healed by Liudger between 787 and 793; alive in the rising of about 793; died 'old and full of days', the year not known (?)
cast.trait: Loved by his neighbours because he is courteous and knows the deeds of the men of old and the wars of kings by heart; kept the secret of his healing as he was told.
cast.want: To keep both: the old kings' stories, and the psalms Liudger is teaching him.
cast.fear: The dark coming back.
cast.voice: Easy and courteous; begins every answer with a story about a king.
cast.looks: About sixty, big-framed and gentle, white hair to the shoulder, eyes that look a little past you from habit, a blue-grey cloak, a stick he no longer needs; his wife leads him by the sleeve out of long use.

ties.note: who healed him
they know the same stories
the island priest asks him for the old names of things

cast.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.25-26: 'antiquorum actus regumque certamina bene noverat psallendo promere'; he baptised eighteen dying infants in the rising, learned the psalms, and his wife died fifteen days after him. Helewyret lies across the Ems mouth from Emuthon, the nearest port. The game's music is set aside for now: he tells.

cast.name: Landric
cast.dates: son of a chief of Fosetesland (Heligoland); baptised by Liudger about 791 (?); ordained priest and 'for many years set over the teaching of the Frisians'
cast.trait: Island-born: knows the old rites from the inside and preaches against them without scorn.
cast.want: A church that stays standing on Fosite's island; his father's people left alone by both kings.
cast.fear: Danish ships at the island; being called a traitor to his father's gods by people he baptised.
cast.voice: Slow and careful; uses sea words for holy things.
cast.looks: Thirty, weathered like a fisherman under the tonsure, a priest's dark tunic, a seal-skin cloak against the rain, a small wooden box with the oil and the host.

ties.note: who lifted him from the font
asks him the old names

cast.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.22. Only his birth, baptism and priesthood are recorded: the rest is ours

cast.name: Hamacar
cast.dates: bishop of Utrecht about 790-806 in the bishops' list; nothing else is known of him (?)
cast.trait: Keeper of Willibrord's house and its school: careful, formal, more a steward of lands than a preacher (our reading; the sources are silent).
cast.want: Wax, wine and oil for Saint Martin's; a ship that will carry letters to York and bring books back.
cast.fear: The East Frisian rising reaching the Vecht; the count taking the church's fines.
cast.voice: Formal; speaks of the blessed Willibrord as of a neighbour who has stepped out.
cast.looks: About fifty, tonsured, a white linen alb under a dark wool cloak, a bishop's ring and a plain staff with a curled head, a deacon with a book beside him.

ties.note: bishop and count dispute every fine
Liudger was schooled in his church

cast.source: Wikipedia 'List of bishops and archbishops of Utrecht': Hamacarus, 790-806. The man is real; his character here is invented

cast.name: Eanbald
cast.dates: Eanbald II: archbishop of York from August 796 (the pallium in 797), last heard of in 808. His predecessor of the same name died on 10 August 796
cast.trait: Alcuin's pupil made a lord: keeps more armed men about him than his old master thinks an archbishop should, and shelters the king's enemies.
cast.want: Books back from Francia for the minster's library; the upper hand over King Eardwulf.
cast.fear: The king.
cast.voice: Quick, with schoolroom Latin tags; impatient with merchants unless they carry letters.
cast.looks: About forty, vigorous, tonsured, a white woollen band (the pallium) over a rich dark vestment on feast days, a riding cloak and spurs on others, thegns at his back.

ties.note: his master, who writes to rebuke his retinue
Ecgwulf is one of the thegns under his protection

cast.source: Alcuin's letters to Eanbald II (MGH Epistolae IV nos. 114, 232-233) (?); Wikipedia 'Eardwulf of Northumbria' (Eardwulf consecrated at York on 26 May 796 by Eanbald I)

cast.name: Æthelheard
cast.dates: archbishop of Canterbury 792/3 to 12 May 805; fled Kent during Eadberht Praen's rising, 796-798; at Rome 801-803
cast.trait: Offa's man in a Kentish see, and the Kentish know it: learned, cautious, in exile when Kent rises.
cast.want: Canterbury's old rank made whole against Offa's new archbishop at Lichfield; a safe crossing to Rome.
cast.fear: The men of Kent.
cast.voice: Measured; says 'the king' and means the Mercian one.
cast.looks: About fifty, tonsured, the pallium over a dark vestment, a crozier, a train of clerks with a book chest; on the road a plain travelling cloak and a mule.

ties.note: Alcuin writes to him in his flight and tells him to go back
both are Offa's men

cast.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (Kent's rising under Eadberht Praen, 796-798; the archbishop's journey to Rome, 799 for 801); the council of Clofesho of 803 ended the archbishopric of Lichfield. Dates of office as commonly given (?)

cast.name: Godfred
cast.dates: king of the Danes; first named in 804; killed by one of his own men in 810
cast.trait: Proud and exact: counts his ships against the emperor's and builds a wall across a neck of land.
cast.want: The toll of every ship between the two seas; Frisia and Saxony as his own provinces.
cast.fear: Nothing he would name. He should have feared his own following.
cast.voice: Short and public; never alone; speaks to merchants through a spokesman.
cast.looks: In his forties, tall, long fair hair combed back, a red cloak with a great gilt pin, gold arm rings, a sword with a silvered hilt; always shown among armed men, horses and ships.

ties.note: has him murdered at Reric in 809
carried him off from Reric
the dealer sells what the king's wars take
his son

cast.source: Annales regni Francorum 804, 808, 809, 810; Einhard, Vita Karoli c. 14; chronicle_793.json. He is at Sliesthorp in 804 and 808; where he kept his hall is not recorded (?)

cast.name: Thrasco
cast.dates: prince (dux) of the Obodrites from about 795, after Witzan was killed by Saxons; beat the Saxons beyond the Elbe in 798; given their land in 804; driven out by Godfred in 808; murdered at Reric in 809
cast.trait: The emperor's friend among the heathen, and proud of it: a fighter who keeps his word to the Franks and his own gods at home.
cast.want: Frankish swords for his men, which the law forbids from 805; the Saxons' land beyond the Elbe.
cast.fear: Godfred's ships in the bay, and the Wilzi at his back.
cast.voice: Courteous to Franks, through an interpreter; does not swear lightly.
cast.looks: About forty, broad, dark hair cut round and a long moustache, a fur-lined cloak with a Frankish sword the emperor gave him, a belt set with silver, guards with round shields and spears.

ties.note: who drives him out and has him killed
takes his toll and his advice

cast.source: Annales regni Francorum 795, 798, 804, 808, 809 (chronicle_793.json 795-summer-witzin-killed, 809-winter-thrasco-murdered). Some reckon his death in 810 (Wikipedia 'Thrasco'). The sword from the emperor is ours

cast.name: Bresal
cast.dates: Bresal son of Segene, abbot of Iona for thirty-one years; died 801
cast.trait: Thirty years abbot of Columba's island: has buried kings who came to die as pilgrims, and sees the first sails from the north in his last years.
cast.want: The island's peace; vellum and wine; word of Lindisfarne, Columba's daughter house.
cast.fear: A sail from the north: Iona is plundered in 795.
cast.voice: Few words, the blessing first; Irish, with Latin for anything that must be exact.
cast.looks: Very old, small, the Roman crown tonsure (his house gave up the old Irish one in 716), an undyed wool habit, a plain staff with a crook, a book satchel hung on a peg behind him.

ties.note: Lindisfarne was founded from Iona; they pray for each other's dead
the abbot who comes after him, at one remove

cast.source: Annals of Ulster 801 (chronicle_793.json 801-bresal); 795 (795-iona-plundered). Iona took the Roman Easter and tonsure in 716 (Bede, Historia ecclesiastica V.22)

cast.name: Cellach
cast.dates: abbot of Iona 802-814; builds the new house at Kells from 807 after sixty-eight of the community are killed in 806; resigns in 814; died 815
cast.trait: The abbot who moved the house: practical, counts hands and boats, will not leave the island empty.
cast.want: Timber, stone and safe hulls to carry Columba's relics and books to Ireland.
cast.fear: To be remembered as the abbot under whom Iona ended.
cast.voice: Brisk; gives a blessing and an order in the same breath.
cast.looks: About fifty, strong, tonsured, sleeves rolled, a habit hitched up for work, a wax tablet with a building's plan scratched on it, monks carrying a carved stone behind him.

ties.note: Bresal's house, which he inherits after Connachtach

cast.source: Annals of Ulster 802, 806, 807, 814 (chronicle_793.json 802-iona-burned, 806-iona-68-killed, 814-cellach-resigns). Kells lies inland in Ireland, north-west of Duiblinn

cast.name: Anskar
cast.dates: born 8 September 801 near Corbie; to the Danes in 826; at Birka 829-831 and again about 852; archbishop at Hamburg 831, at Bremen from 848; died 3 February 865
cast.trait: A visionary and a stubborn one: buys boys out of slavery to make them priests, gives gifts before he asks, travels in merchants' ships.
cast.want: A church and a bell at Sliaswic, a priest at Birka, and the leave of kings who can take it back.
cast.fear: That the work will die with him.
cast.voice: Soft and patient; never argues with a king in public.
cast.looks: As first met, twenty-five, thin, tonsured, a monk's black habit worn at the hem, barefoot in the boat; later a greying archbishop in a hair shirt under a plain cloak, the pallium only at the altar.

ties.note: his first great convert
wins him with gifts and talk
one of his flock at Birka

cast.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii (tr. Robinson 1921) c. 7-12, 15-16, 24-27, 31-32, 35; Wikipedia 'Ansgar' for the dates

cast.name: Herigar
cast.dates: prefect of Birka and a counsellor of the king; baptised about 830; died about 851, before Anskar's second coming
cast.trait: The keeper of the town, baptised, with a church on his own land; argues with the assembly in the rain and stays dry; blunt as a judge.
cast.want: A priest at Birka again after 845.
cast.fear: The town paying for his faith: when the exiled king Anound came with Danish ships, the merchants bought peace with a hundred pounds of silver.
cast.voice: Blunt; a townsman who talks like a lawman.
cast.looks: About fifty, heavy, a grey beard, a fur-trimmed cloak with a ring pin, a small silver cross worn openly, a staff of office, warehouse keys.

ties.note: who baptised him
the two pillars of Birka's Christians

cast.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 11, 19 (tr. Robinson 1921): 'the prefect of this town named Herigar, who was a counsellor of the king'

cast.name: Frideburg
cast.dates: a rich Christian widow of Birka; old when the priest was driven out in 845; died about 852-855, after the hermit Ardgar came (?)
cast.trait: Rich, old and unbending: with no priest left in Birka she kept bought wine by her for three years, to be given her at the last in place of the sacrament.
cast.want: Everything she owns given to the poor; and since Birka has few poor, carried to Dorstadt, where there are many.
cast.fear: Dying without the last rites.
cast.voice: Dry and certain; quotes her own promises back to people.
cast.looks: Past seventy, upright in a chair, a fine dark gown with silver oval brooches and beads of glass and carnelian, a small cross among them, a sealed jar of wine on the shelf behind her.

ties.note: her daughter
the other pillar of Birka's Christians

cast.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 20 (tr. Robinson 1921)

cast.name: Catla
cast.dates: Frideburg's daughter; carried her mother's wealth from Birka to Dorestad after her death, about 852-860 (?)
cast.trait: Dutiful and practical: she does exactly what her mother asked, and when she and her helpers are weary she buys four pennies' worth of wine and goes on.
cast.want: To give it all away in the right places and go home.
cast.fear: The road: the way to Dorstadt is beset by pirates.
cast.voice: Counts aloud; asks devout women, not men, whom she can trust.
cast.looks: About forty, sunburned from the voyage, a plain travelling cloak over a good gown, her mother's beads, a heavy leather bag she carries herself and keeps on her lap.

ties.note: her mother
his flock at Birka

cast.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 20: 'There are there many churches, priests, and clergy, and a multitude of poor people'; the bag found full again but for 'the four denarii' (tr. Robinson 1921)

cast.name: Rorik
cast.dates: a Dane of the royal kin; held Dorestad with his brother Harald under Louis the Pious; fled Lothar about 844; took Dorestad in 850 and was granted it; driven out by the Cokingi in 867 and back by 870; last heard of in 873; dead by 882
cast.trait: A sea-raider made a count: keeps his oath for as long as it keeps him, and keeps other raiders off the river better than the emperor could.
cast.want: The tolls of Dorestad, and a kingdom in Denmark if one comes loose.
cast.fear: A stronger fleet than his own; the Frisians who drive him out in 867.
cast.voice: Courteous Frankish with a Danish turn; bargains like a merchant and remembers like a king.
cast.looks: As granted the town, about forty: tall, fair, a moustache, a Frankish count's cloak and sword-belt over a northern tunic, gold arm rings, a ship's prow behind him; a cross on his breast by the 860s.

ties.note: his man at the toll
king of the Danes, whose kingdom he tries for in 855-857

cast.source: Annales Bertiniani 850, 863, 867, 870, 872; Annales Fuldenses 850, 857; Annales Xantenses 873 (chronicle_793.json 850-rorik-dorestad; Wikipedia 'Rorik of Dorestad'). A letter of Hincmar of Reims addresses him as a convert about 863 (Flodoard) (?): faith old_gods before, christian after

cast.name: Horik
cast.dates: Horik I, son of Godfred; one of the kings of the Danes from 813, sole king from about 827; killed in a civil war in 854
cast.trait: Godfred's son, who learned what his father's pride cost: disowns the fleets that burn Dorestad, takes the bishop's gifts, lets a church be built and stays unbaptised.
cast.want: The emperor's friendship on his own terms; Frisia, if it is offered.
cast.fear: His own nephews.
cast.voice: Guarded; answers a question with a gift.
cast.looks: In age: grey, heavy, a king's red cloak and gold arm rings, a hall full of benches and shields behind him, a bishop's gift of Frankish glass on the table.

ties.note: his father
gives him the plot for the church at Sliaswic
an exile of the royal kin with a fleet

cast.source: Annales regni Francorum 813-827; Annales Bertiniani 836, 838 (he denies sending the fleets and asks for the Frisians and Obodrites); Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 24, 31; chronicle_793.json 854-horik-killed

cast.name: Ohthere
cast.dates: a Northman of Halogaland who told King Alfred of his voyages about 890
cast.trait: Rich by northern reckoning, six hundred tame reindeer and the tribute of the Finnas, and a careful witness: says what he saw himself and marks what he was only told.
cast.want: A market in the south for walrus ivory and ship's rope of hide; to know how far north the land runs.
cast.fear: Not recorded. (Ours: the Cwenas, who carry their boats over the mountains to raid.)
cast.voice: Understated; measures everything in days' sail and says which hand the land was on.
cast.looks: About fifty, tall, weather-dark, a walrus-ivory comb and knife handle, a cloak of fine marten, a coil of hide rope and a pair of tusks carried behind him as a gift for a king.

ties.note: their two accounts were written down together for the same king

cast.source: The Old English Orosius (texts_793.json ohthere; chronicle_793.json 890-ohthere-wulfstan). He lived 'northmost of all Northmen'; Skiringssal is where he sails to, a month's sail south. Where he met Alfred is not recorded (?)

cast.name: Wulfstan
cast.dates: sailed from Hedeby to Truso in seven days and nights and told King Alfred of it, about 890
cast.trait: A seaman with an eye for other people's customs: the Este's drinking, their kings, the horse-race for a dead man's goods, the cold they can make in summer.
cast.want: Amber and a fair wind home.
cast.fear: Not recorded.
cast.voice: Lists the lands to port and to starboard like a rope of knots.
cast.looks: Around forty, a sea cloak, a trimmed beard, an English knife with an inlaid blade, a string of rough amber just bought.

ties.note: their accounts stand side by side

cast.source: The Old English Orosius (texts_793.json wulfstan). Whether he was an Englishman, or a Dane or Frisian with an Englished name, is not known (?)

cast.name: Rollo
cast.dates: a leader of the Northmen on the Seine; granted Rouen and the land about it by King Charles the Simple in 911 and baptised; dead by about 930 (?)
cast.trait: A raider who took a river and kept it: gives his men land by the rope, hangs thieves, and lets the archbishop back into his city.
cast.want: The Seine quiet under his own peace, and its tolls.
cast.fear: Other Northmen coming up his river.
cast.voice: Few words, in Norse or through a Frankish clerk; a promise is short and kept.
cast.looks: Old, very big, grey-bearded, a Frankish cloak and sword over northern dress, an arm ring, a new and awkward cross; behind him Rouen's Roman walls and a row of ships drawn up.
cast.source: A charter of Charles the Simple of 14 March 918 speaks of land granted 'to the Northmen of the Seine, namely Rollo and his companions' (our rendering); Flodoard for the grants of 924 and 933; Dudo of Saint-Quentin (about 1015, LATER) for the treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte and most of the story. Dudo makes him a Dane; Norse tradition (13th century) a Norwegian, Hrolf the Walker (?). chronicle_793.json 911-rollo-rouen

cast.name: Cnut
cast.dates: born about 995; chosen king by the Danish fleet in 1014; king of all England from 30 November 1016, of Denmark from about 1018, of Norway from 1028; at Rome in 1027; died 12 November 1035
cast.trait: A conqueror who becomes a careful Christian king: pays off his fleet, keeps forty ships, gives to churches, and bargains with emperors over merchants' tolls.
cast.want: One peace on both shores of the North Sea, and his merchants free of unjust tolls on the road to Rome.
cast.fear: What happens to it all when he dies.
cast.voice: Formal, through writs and reeves; a merchant hears him as a law read out.
cast.looks: About thirty, tall, fair, a long nose (so later writers say (?)), a crown and a gold-hilted sword on feast days, housecarls with gilded axes behind him.

ties.note: his greatest earl, outlawed in 1021 and reconciled in 1023

cast.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1014-1035; Cnut's letter of 1027 on the tolls; chronicle_793.json 1016-10-18-assandun, 1018-heregeld, 1027-03-26-cnut-rome, 1035-11-12-cnut-dies

cast.name: Thorkell
cast.dates: Thorkell the Tall: brings his army to Sandwich in 1009; takes Æthelred's pay with 45 ships from 1012; Cnut's earl in East Anglia from 1017; outlawed 1021, reconciled 1023
cast.trait: A sea-king for hire: takes East Kent's three thousand pounds, tries to buy the archbishop's life from his own drunken men, then sells his ships to the English king.
cast.want: Pay, and a lord worth serving.
cast.fear: His own army at a feast.
cast.voice: Loud, open-handed, sudden.
cast.looks: Very tall, in his forties, a long moustache, a mail shirt and a gilded helmet, a great axe, forty-five ships at anchor behind him in the Thames.

ties.note: after 1016

cast.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1009-1023; Thietmar of Merseburg VII.42-43 for his offer to ransom Archbishop Ælfheah (?); chronicle_793.json 1009-08-thorkell, 1012-04-19-aelfheah. His faith is not recorded (?)

aliases.note: Thread ids that were named in the interim file of 4 Oct and are folded into another thread: use the id on the right.

tone.note: Five lines in the game's voice, each with who says it and why it is right; then five things never to write. Plain words a clever person of any time would say; the humour is dry and is the period's own (Design/content/BRIEF.md rule 3).

lines.who: the game, telling a fact (the Chronicle's flat, dated voice)
lines.text: This year, before Saint John's day, heathen men came to the holy island, and the bishop counted what was gone.
lines.why: A year, a feast for the date, what happened, no adjective doing the work. Model: the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (texts_793.json chronicle_793).

lines.who: a Frisian toll man at Dorestad
lines.text: A tenth to the king. The rest is yours, if the river lets you keep it.
lines.why: A Frisian is dry: he says the hard thing first and plainly, and the joke is that it is true.

lines.who: a Dane, home from the west
lines.text: The crossing was wet. We lost the mast, and Thorir.
lines.why: A Northman says less than he means: understatement, the worst thing last and smallest.

lines.who: an English scribe at Gyrwe, to a merchant
lines.text: The ink freezes, my hand shakes, and the abbot wants the psalter by Easter. Have you wax? Have you news of York?
lines.why: A monk's complaint from the margin of his page, and homesickness for books and for home; he wants concrete things.

lines.text: Forty skins. I counted them at Aldeigjuborg and again this morning. Forty. Now weigh your silver where I can see the scale.
lines.why: A Svea counts everything twice; the talk is of numbers, weights and things, never of feelings.

never: Mock-old or modern speech: no thee and thou, no 'aye', 'verily' or 'my lord merchant'; no 'okay', 'deal', 'no problem'; no joke with a punchline, and nothing that winks at the player or knows what comes after its own year.

The wrong names for people and things: never 'Viking' as a people (Northmen, Danes, heathen men; 'wicing' only for a raider at sea), never 'adventure', 'quest', 'loot' or 'tavern' in a speaker's mouth; no horned helmets, compasses, charts, clocks, chimneys, buttons or forks; ale-house, not inn.

Numbers a person of 793 would not say: no month dates ('the ninth of October'), no clock hours, no miles, no percentages. Say the feast, the moon, the tide, the days' sail; a share as a tenth or a third; the odds as sure, likely or doubtful.

Sermons and history lessons: nobody explains their own age, their faith or their law at length. Faith is ordinary and brief (a fast day, a relic, a hammer under a shirt beside a cross); no speaker judges slavery, the old gods or the king with the eyes of a later time, and no card only punishes.

Anything untrue to its year or its source: no quotation from a modern book, game or translation (only texts_793.json and translations free to use, credited); no real person given invented deeds without saying so in 'source'; no invented person with a real person's name and office; no coin of the north before about 825, no Norse Dublin before 841, no Danelaw before 878, no tribute called Danegeld before 991, no Normandy before 911.

calendar.note: The days every writer uses. Dates are Julian, as the chronicle's. People say a day by its feast, a week by the moon, a season by the work. 'certain' true means the feast or custom is attested for the 790s in the place named; false means it is likely, or known only from a later source (the note says which). The engine knows the feasts in Code/Runtime/Levels/Feasts.cs (Easter by the computus, Good Friday, Ascension, Pentecost, New Year, Epiphany, Candlemas, Saint John's eve and day, Peter and Paul, the Assumption, Michaelmas, All Saints, Martinmas, Christmas eve and day).

easter.rule: Easter falls between 22 March and 25 April. Ash Wednesday is 46 days before it, Ascension 39 days after, Pentecost 49 days after.
easter.source: the Julian computus as in Feasts.cs; the game's first day, 21 June 793, is three days before Saint John's

days.name: Epiphany (Twelfth Day)
days.use: The end of the Christmas feasting; in 878 the Danes fall on Chippenham just after it.
days.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 36; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 878

days.name: Candlemas (the Purification)
days.use: Every church wants wax; wax is dearest in January.

days.name: The Disting at Uppsalir
days.when: late winter, in the month of Goi (February to March)
days.use: A thing of all the Svear with a market and a sacrifice to the disir, while the ice still bears sledges. LATER: Snorri, 13th century.

days.name: Lent
days.when: Ash Wednesday to Easter eve, forty fast days
days.use: No meat: fish is wanted everywhere, and a Saxon who eats meat can die for it under the first Saxon law. The sea is still shut; boats are tarred.
days.source: Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 4; research_trade_seasons_and_hints.md 1

days.name: Saint Cuthbert
days.use: The island's own day; pilgrims at the shrine.
days.source: Bede, Vita Cuthberti; the Lindisfarne calendar

days.name: The Annunciation (Lady Day)
days.use: Spring sowing; in many places the year is reckoned from here or from Christmas.

days.name: Easter
days.use: The great feast and the end of the fast: wine for every altar, new clothes, and the sea opens. The game's sailing season runs from Easter to Martinmas. The king keeps Easter at a palace (Noviomagus in some years) and the counts go to him.
days.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 36 (Easter week kept whole); Design/research_indie_and_concept.md 4.4

days.name: The first day of summer in the north
days.use: The ships are launched; an offering for victory and a good season. LATER: the three yearly sacrifices are Snorri's (Ynglinga saga c. 8).

days.name: The Greater Litany
days.use: A procession through the fields with relics; no trading while it passes.

days.name: The raiding season
days.when: about 1 May to the end of September
days.use: The game's raiders are out between these days (Plans/ai_fleets.md). Lindisfarne fell on 8 June.

days.name: The king's assembly and the host
days.when: May to July, where the king is
days.use: The great men gather and the army marches from it (to Saxony most years to 804): grain, horses and carts are bought up along its road, and counts are away from home.
days.source: Annales regni Francorum year by year (chronicle_793.json: 794 Frankfurt, 795 Kostheim)

days.name: The Rogation days
days.who: Frankish churches; the English since the council of Clofesho, 747 (?)
days.use: Three days of fasting and processions for the crops, then Ascension Thursday.

days.name: Pentecost (Whitsun)
days.use: Kept like Easter, a whole week; a day for baptisms.

days.name: Saint Boniface
days.use: The day he was killed at Doccinga in 754: a gathering at his church there.

days.name: Saint Columba
days.use: The island's own feast.

days.name: Saint John the Baptist (midsummer)
days.when: 24 June; fires on the eve, 23 June
days.use: The game's first feast: three days after the start. Fires on the eve are well known later and likely now (?). Nantes is stormed on this day in 843.

days.name: The summer markets of the north
days.use: The seasonal markets are full: beads, combs, furs, cloth, wine, people. Outside these weeks a northern landing may be half empty.
days.source: fairs_793.json (the digs at Ribe and Kaupang; dates are the game's) (?)

days.name: Saints Peter and Paul
days.use: A feast day; Rome's own, dear to the English.

days.name: Lammas (loaf-mass)
days.use: The first loaf of the new corn is blessed; grain prices break as the harvest comes in. The name is in English writing from the 9th century, so likely in 793 (?). In Ireland the fair of Tailtiu is held by the king of Tara at this season (the Annals of Ulster note the year it was not held, 811).

days.name: The Assumption of Saint Mary
days.use: Harvest in full swing; honey is taken.

days.name: The herring
days.who: the English east coast and the North Sea
days.use: The shoals come inshore; salt is wanted by the boatload, and the barrels are cheap by November.
days.source: seasons_793.json (a guess shaped by later sources)

days.name: Michaelmas: the count's day
days.use: The day the house's debt falls due (the game's rule). Rents and dues are reckoned after harvest; the autumn gales begin.
days.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 36 (the feast); Design/DECISIONS.md no. 10 (the debt)

days.name: Saint Remigius; Saint Bavo at Ganda
days.use: A Frankish feast of the first rank, and Ganda's own saint's day; the vintage begins on the Rhine.

days.name: The fair of Saint-Denis
days.use: English ('Saxon') and Frisian merchants sell wool and cloth and buy wine and honey; the abbey takes the tolls. The riddle chain salt_to_pepper pays here.
days.source: Pippin's judgement of 753 on the fair's tolls (the 'charter of Dagobert' is a later forgery); fairs_793.json

days.name: The winter nights
days.use: The start of winter: a feast and an offering for a good year; raiders are home. LATER: saga accounts.

days.name: All Saints
days.who: the English and Irish; the Franks only from about 800
days.use: Alcuin urges it on his Frankish friends about 800 and Louis the Pious orders it kept everywhere in 835: before that do not put it in a Frankish mouth. York falls on this day in 866.

days.name: Saint Willibrord
days.use: The day he died in 739: Utrecht's founder.

days.name: Martinmas
days.who: all Christians; Traiectum above all, whose church is Saint Martin's
days.use: The sea closes: the end of the game's sailing year. The slaughter month: salt is dearest, hides and tallow cheap, the new wine comes down the Rhine.
days.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 36; Bede, De temporum ratione c. 15 (Blotmonath); research_trade_seasons_and_hints.md 1

days.name: The fast before Christmas
days.when: from Martinmas or from late November to Christmas eve
days.use: Fish again; how long the fast runs differs from church to church (?).

days.name: Christmas
days.use: Four days kept whole, twelve of feasting. The Frankish annals turn the year here. Charles is crowned emperor on this day in 800, William king in 1066: the end of the game.

days.name: Yule
days.use: Ale brewed and drunk, pork, oaths sworn; the old English held 'Mothers' Night' at the same turn of the year (Bede). The exact night is not known for 793: Snorri says the heathen Yule was at midwinter night and was moved to Christmas about 950. LATER.
days.source: Bede, De temporum ratione c. 15; Snorri, Hakonar saga goda c. 13 (13th century) (?)

days.name: The thing at Birka
days.when: not recorded; in the sailing season when the king is there (?)
days.use: The assembly of the town, where the king must put a matter to the people and the lot is cast: 'It is our custom that the control of public business of every kind should rest with the whole people and not with the king' (the king's answer to Anskar, tr. Robinson 1921).

days.name: The count's court
days.when: three general courts a year, and lesser ones between (?)
days.use: Where a suit is heard, an oath sworn with oath-helpers and a fine set: the 'law hearing' of the cards. Frisian law is spoken by wise men (Lex Frisionum).
days.source: Carolingian capitularies on the placita (?); Lex Frisionum, about 802

days.name: The Saxons' assembly at Marklo
days.when: once a year, by the Weser
days.who: the Old Saxons, before the conquest
days.use: A memory by 793: the yearly meeting of the districts' men, forbidden by the first Saxon law (c. 34: no general assemblies). The crew's Brunger has heard of it from his father.
days.source: Vita Lebuini antiqua (9th-10th century, of about 770: LATER); Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 34

days.name: The Althing of Iceland
days.use: For the later ages only.

days.name: Sunday
days.use: No market on a Sunday except where it is an old custom (from 809); no work. A port card should not open a market on a Sunday without saying why.

days.name: The fasts of the four seasons, and Wednesdays and Fridays
days.when: a Wednesday, Friday and Saturday in each season; among the Irish every Wednesday and Friday
days.use: Small fasts aboard and ashore: a pious crewman keeps them, a heathen one does not (npc_text_encounters.md sample 22).
days.source: common church custom; for the Irish the Rule of Tallaght (9th century) (?)

days.name: The moon and the tide
days.use: The tide follows the moon, and high water comes at a different hour in each port; springs at full and new moon. A skipper names a day as 'the third night of the new moon'.

gods_and_faith.note: What a person of each people would actually say or do about God or the gods in 793: two sentences each, with the source. 'later' true means the best source was written long after 793 and must not be put in a mouth of 793 as fact. Faith is ordinary and brief in the game: a feast, a fast, an oath, a thing worn under a shirt.

peoples.says: A Frank swears by Saint Martin and Saint Denis, pays his tithe because the king's law now makes him, and holds that the king's wars on the heathen are God's work. His priest still has to forbid him the old things: charms tied on, auguries from birds and horses, feasts at graves and vows at springs, trees and stones.
peoples.source: Capitulary of Herstal 779 c. 7 (tithes); Admonitio generalis 789 c. 65 (against enchanters, weather-makers and vows at trees, stones and springs) (?); Indiculus superstitionum et paganiarum (a list of about 743 in a manuscript of about 800, Vatican Pal. lat. 577)

peoples.says: A Frisian west of the Lauwers is two generations baptised, keeps Boniface's day at Doccinga, and tells how King Radbod drew his foot back from the font rather than be parted from his fathers; east of the Lauwers the churches burned as lately as 793. He remembers that Fosite's spring was drawn in silence, and that the old law gave a man who robbed a shrine to the sea, at the tide line, to the gods he had wronged.
peoples.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.22; Alcuin, Vita Willibrordi c. 10; Lex Frisionum, Additio sapientum XI (about 802); the story of Radbod at the font is in the Vita Vulframni c. 9 (early 9th century) (?)

peoples.says: A Saxon has said the vow, 'I forsake all the devil's works and words, Thunaer and Woden and Saxnot', because since about 785 the law is baptism or death, and it is death too to eat meat in Lent or to burn the dead. He pays the tithe and keeps quiet, and some still go to the springs and groves that the same law names.
peoples.source: The Old Saxon baptismal vow (texts_793.json saxon_vow; Vatican Pal. lat. 577); Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 4, 7, 8, 21 (about 782-785), softened by the Capitulare Saxonicum of 797

peoples.says: An Englishman's people have been Christian five or six generations: he counts time by saints' days, gives to his minster, and has kings who went to Rome to die. Yet monks still listen at table to stories of the old heathen kings, so that Alcuin asks what Ingeld has to do with Christ, and in 786 the pope's legates had to forbid the English to cast lots, eat horse and mark their bodies as the heathen do.
peoples.source: Alcuin's letter of 797 to a bishop he calls Speratus, once taken to be Higbald (MGH Epistolae IV no. 124: 'Quid Hinieldus cum Christo?'); the legates' report of 786, c. 19 (MGH Epistolae IV no. 3) (?); Bede, De temporum ratione c. 15, for the old English months and Mothers' Night

peoples.says: A Dane gives the gods their due at the turns of the year and asks them by lot before a voyage or a war; an oath on the holy ring binds him as nothing else does, and what he wants to leave behind is a good name. If his king allows it he will hear a Christian priest out, and take the sign of the cross as a guest's courtesy, without leaving his own gods.
peoples.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 876 (the Danes swear to Alfred on the holy ring; Giles 1847 has 'bracelet'); Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 19, 24 (lots among the Danes; men 'willingly signed with the cross' at Sliaswic who put off baptism); Hávamál 76-77 for the name that never dies (Bellows 1923: texts_793.json havamal_076, havamal_077; written down about 1270, older in substance); Thietmar of Merseburg I.17 on a nine-yearly sacrifice at Lejre is of about 1015 and LATER

peoples.says: A Svea asks the gods by lot whether a thing may be done, and holds that a matter for the whole people is settled at the thing and not by the king. His gods must be useful: at Birka in the 850s they offered, through a man who said he had been at their meeting, to take the dead King Eric among them if the people wanted more gods, and an old man answered that Christ had helped men in peril at sea.
peoples.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 26-27 (tr. Robinson 1921), of about 852. The temple at Uppsala with Thor, Wodan and Fricco and the feast every nine years is Adam of Bremen IV.26-27, written about 1075: LATER, never as fact for 793

peoples.says: A Wend of the Obodrites keeps his gods in groves no stranger may enter, takes his people's decisions in assembly, asks the lot, and holds an oath a dangerous thing, not lightly sworn. Nothing written of his worship is as old as 793: the accounts are a Saxon bishop's and a Saxon priest's, two and four centuries on.
peoples.source: Thietmar of Merseburg VI.23-25 (about 1018, on the Liutizi and Riedegost: the sacred wood, lots, the horse oracle, the assembly that must agree); Helmold, Chronica Slavorum I.52, I.84 (about 1170: the grove of Prove; the Slavs 'most unwilling to swear') (?). The Annales regni Francorum say only that the Obodrites were heathen and the Franks' allies. The brief's 'oaths sworn on water' is not in these sources (?)

peoples.says: An Irish monk fasts on Wednesdays and Fridays, sings the psalms through, and counts leaving his own land for God the best road there is: brothers of his have sailed to islands in the northern ocean where the midsummer night is light enough to pick the lice from a shirt.
